Proposal title: Build Agentic RAG Routing Systems that decide like humans
Abstract:
Agents promise autonomous task automation, but without purpose-built query routing, they devolve into expensive, unreliable black boxes. This talk addresses a critical gap: how to design Agentic RAG systems that intelligently determine when to utilize internal knowledge versus external tools (e.g., web search)—without hallucinating or incurring API credits.

In my talk, I will also cover the importance of Intent behind the user query and route it accordingly so that a better response is generated to the given user query. For the hands-on demo, participants will build a live use case, where they will create a Knowledge base RAG using Python frameworks like LlamaIndex and Python Qdrant-client. The routing engine logic is inspired by the Nvidia LLM Router.
Description: AI agents often struggle with deciding when to rely on internal knowledge versus calling external tools, leading to unreliable responses and unnecessary API costs. This talk tackles that head-on by diving into how to design Agentic RAG systems with purpose-built query routing. We'll explore how understanding user intent plays a key role in routing queries effectively.
Notes: This will be a complete Hands-on workshop where participants will write code along with me.
What motivates you to submit this propos: - I have been an active PyCon speaker in Malaysia, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Indonesia, and delivering talks to the community motivates me.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth:
- LLM and Agent are widely adopted in the Python language. Since the industry is moving towards AI-powered applications in their organization, knowing cost-cutting is very important. 
- Intent classification and Routing are critical concepts in building Agentic and LLM-based applications.
What value will the audience gain?:
- Importance of routing in AI Agents and LLM-based applications. 
- How to build a routing engine using ReAcT agent capability, i.e., Reasoning and Action (ReAcT).

Proposal title: UV – Python Packaging at the Speed of Light
Abstract:
If you've ever wondered why installing Python packages takes so long—or why packaging workflows are so scattered—you’re not alone. In recent years, tools like pip, poetry, pipenv, and pyenv have all tried to solve pieces of this problem.
uv, developed by the team behind the lightning-fast linter Ruff, is a new Python package manager written in Rust. It’s designed to be a drop-in replacement for pip and pip-tools, but it goes far beyond: creating and managing virtual environments, installing Python itself, and eventually evolving into a full project manager (like Cargo for Rust).
Description:
This talk will walk you through:

Why Python packaging needed a rethink

How uv works under the hood to achieve huge speedups (up to 100x faster in some cases)

How to replace your existing tools with uv, step-by-step

What the future of Python packaging might look like with uv and Rye

I’ll demo how you can adopt uv in real-world projects today, including for Django apps, CLI tools, and scripts. By the end, you'll be equipped to ditch your old tools and level up your workflow—with no loss in functionality and massive gains in speed.
What motivates you to submit this propos: When I discovered how fast and efficient uv is, it felt like a game-changer. I submitted this proposal to help others break out of old, inefficient workflows and realize that modern tooling doesn't have to be painful. The Python community deserves packaging tools that are fast, reliable, and pleasant to use — and uv is a huge step in that direction.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Packaging is a core part of every Python developer’s workflow, yet it’s often overlooked until something breaks. Tools like uv and Rye are not just incremental improvements — they represent a rethink of how dependency management and environment setup should work in Python. By making packaging dramatically faster and more predictable, we remove a major source of friction for developers. This talk brings attention to a foundational improvement that impacts everything from web apps to data science workflows.
What value will the audience gain?:
The audience will:

Learn why traditional Python packaging has struggled, and where tools like pip, virtualenv, and Poetry fall short in terms of performance and UX.

Gain a clear, practical understanding of how uv works and why it’s so fast.

See step-by-step instructions for adopting uv in real-world projects, including Django apps and CLI tools.

Discover how uv fits with modern tools like Rye to simplify and speed up workflows.

Leave with the confidence to migrate away from slower legacy tools and adopt modern packaging in their day-to-day development.

This talk is ideal for anyone who’s ever typed pip install and thought, “Why is this taking so long?”

Proposal title: The graph capture mechanisms in PyTorch
Abstract:
PyTorch is the the most popular deep learning framework used in both academic and industry. Researchers and engineers use PyTorch to train their models with the convenient and well-defined neural network APIs in eager mode. After training, one has to export the model computation flow as a graph to a framework-agnostic format (e.g., ONNX, TensorRT, etc.) to deploy the trained model for inference with better performance. Thus, we need a mechanism to capture the computation operations happend inside a DNN model.

Graph capturing aims to track and record the PyTorch API invocations used in a model. Since the release of PyTorch 2.0 in 2023, there are two primary machineries to trace a model computation graph: `fx.symbolic_trace` and Dynamo. In this proposal, I'd like to introduce the usage of both kinds of APIs, and further dissect the underlying working machinary of these two approaches. We also tend to discuss the limitations of both, showing that `fx.symbolic_trace` is limited by the static symbolic tracing mode and Dynamo is still on its early age.

The slides are available: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/12u6sjOJgLeWltmLTzpoNvcR6bUynTZ4iyFwPpPVrRwI/edit?usp=sharing
Description:
In this proposal, I'd like to share the following key topics about the graph capture approaches in PyTorch:
- How can we harness `fx.symbolic_trace` and `torch.dynamo.export` to capture the DNN operations during the model execution
- How does the symbolic trace mechanism from FX produces the static model graph by substituting the substantial tensors in the graph with "fake" symbolic values
- How Dynamo exploits the custom frame evaluation interface provided by CPython since PEP 523 to dynamically evaluate and dump the PyTorch API invocations during eager execution of DNN models, showing that PyTorch not only treats Python as a frontend language, but also deeply leverages CPython runtime features to extend its flexibility and usability
- The respect limitations of both interfaces
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: PyTorch Dynamo is an important feature built atop of PEP 523, which provides an interface to allow developers to evaluate Python frames in their own logic. I think this proves that PyTorch is not a framework only combining Python frontend API plus C/C++/CUDA backend implementation, but one deeply bind to Python ecosystem due to its extendibility.
What value will the audience gain?: A basic understanding how PyTorch graph capturing mechanisms work with CPython features.

Proposal title: Typing Python: Write Code Like a Strongly-Typed Pro
Abstract: > **Ever wondered why large Python codebases become hard to maintain? This talk will show you how to write Python that’s as reliable and readable as any statically-typed language. You’ll learn why type hints matter, how to use them effectively, and how to catch bugs before they happen—without sacrificing Python’s flexibility.**
Description:
> **Python is famously dynamic, but that flexibility can quickly turn into a maintenance nightmare, especially in production. After seeing (and suffering from) real-world Python code with little or no type safety, I set out to find a better way.**
>
> Repo: https://github.com/dominicchandev/pycon-typing-talk
>
> In this practical session, you’ll learn:
>
> - The pain points of untyped Python in production, and why type hints are a game-changer for readability and maintenance.
> - How to use Python’s built-in type hinting system for lists, dicts, tuples, sequences, callables, and more—plus how type info is stored in `__annotations__`.
> - How to install and configure [mypy](http://mypy-lang.org/) to automatically check types in your project.
> - The theory behind strong typing: invariance, covariance, contravariance, and how to use `TypeVar`, `Generic`, and type bounds in real production code.
> - Real-world examples demonstrating how adding type hints can prevent bugs and make code easier to refactor.
>
> Whether you’re new to type hints or want to level up your Python code, you’ll walk away with concrete practices you can apply immediately. Let’s make Python codebases as robust as their strongly-typed cousins!
Notes:
> - This talk is aimed at Python developers of all levels, but some familiarity with function and class syntax is assumed.
> - Live code examples will be presented, including both “bad” real-world code and improved, type-annotated versions.
> - Slides, code samples, and links to further resources (type theory, mypy, static analysis) will be provided after the talk.
> - Questions and audience participation are highly encouraged!
What motivates you to submit this propos: I am motivated by my firsthand experience maintaining and scaling Python codebases in production environments where the absence of type hints led to hard-to-find bugs, costly refactoring, and steep learning curves for new team members. Having seen how type hinting and static analysis tools can transform Python into a language that is both dynamic and robust, I want to share actionable insights and best practices with the community. My goal is to help others write Python that is easier to reason about, safer to refactor, and more enjoyable to maintain.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: As Python continues to dominate in both scripting and large-scale application development, the need for maintainable, reliable, and readable code has never been greater. Static typing bridges the gap between Python’s dynamic nature and the strong guarantees offered by statically-typed languages. By highlighting the practical benefits and sharing best practices, this talk addresses a critical aspect of Python’s evolution—enabling teams and individuals to write code that scales gracefully as projects and teams grow. This topic is timely and essential for keeping Python at the forefront of modern software development.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will gain a concrete roadmap for adopting type hints and static type checking in both new and existing Python projects. The talk will demystify type theory concepts (like variance) in a practical way, empowering developers to catch more bugs before they reach production. By seeing real-world examples from data migration scenarios, participants will learn not just the “how” but also the “why” of typing in Python, leading to stronger, more maintainable, and collaborative codebases across the PyCon community.

Proposal title: Implementing an MCP Server for DBMS in Python — YDB’s Experience
Abstract:
Learn how YDB leverages the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to integrate AI models with database systems. This session explores the development of a Python-based MCP server that facilitates seamless interactions between large language models and YDB’s open-source Distributed SQL database management system. Learn about the design decisions, challenges faced, and the practical benefits of integrating MCP into data architecture. Proposal title: IaC Meets Python: When Terraform Isn't Enough
Abstract: Terraform is powerful—but it has limits. In this talk, we’ll explore where Python can complement infrastructure-as-code (IaC): from dynamic resource creation and complex validations to custom workflows and post-deployment logic. Using real-world SRE/DevOps scenarios, we’ll walk through how Python scripts and tools (like Pulumi, Python CDK, or simple custom wrappers) help close Terraform’s gaps. This session is for anyone building infra who’s hit the wall with HCL and needs flexibility—without abandoning automation.
What motivates you to submit this propos: As an SRE, I've worked extensively with Terraform and have seen how it excels—until it doesn’t. I’ve often needed Python to bridge the gap for complex deployments, validations, or multi-step workflows. I want to share this hybrid approach with others who may be struggling with Terraform’s limitations, and show how Python can empower them to build more reliable, maintainable infrastructure.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is increasingly central to DevOps and infrastructure work, especially as teams seek to go beyond rigid DSLs like HCL. This topic highlights how Python can add flexibility, testability, and extensibility to infrastructure automation. It helps Python developers realize they can play a crucial role in shaping modern infrastructure—without switching languages or tooling ecosystems.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will learn where and how to combine Python with Terraform or other IaC tools to solve real infrastructure problems. They’ll gain concrete examples of dynamic resource handling, validations, and automation scripts that extend IaC capabilities. The talk will leave them with a toolkit of patterns and tools—Pulumi, Python CDK, custom Python wrappers—they can start applying immediately to streamline and scale their infrastructure workflows.

Proposal title: Real-World Pytest: Designing Testable Code and Taming Regressions
Abstract:
Testing the correctness of a software is often the most important task before shipping to production. While Pytest is the most widely used testing framework in Python, it's actual usage in real-world scenario is questionable. Even worse, some tests are written just for increasing enough code coverages but the more important software qualities are often neglected.

In this talk, I will talk about real-world testing concepts and strategies, including designing testable interface in the coding phase, speeding up your test with capture-and-replay frameworks for feedback, and catching code regressions across versions with mock assertions.

This talk is ideal for **intermediate** to **advanced Python developers** who work in teams and care about testing as a tool for stability, speed, and developer confidence. Expect practical takeaways, conceptual demos, and hard-won lessons from real production environments.
Description:
The talk is organized in the following agenda: | Time | Segment | Content | | --------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 0–3 min | **Intro** | Why testing matters in production. Overview of goals: testability, regressions, confidence in code. | | 3–9 min | **Designing Testable Code** | Patterns for writing test-friendly code: parametrization, DI, avoiding hard-coded values.
🔍 *Demo: Refactor to inject parameters for easier testing* | | 9–14 min | **Catching Regressions Effectively** | Building robust test suites using parametrized tests, fixtures, and CI. How to test like your future self will thank you. | | 14–20 min | **Speed Up with `pytest-recording`** | Intro to recording/replaying HTTP and I/O with `pytest-recording`.
🔍 *Demo: Record & replay an API interaction to show speed gains* | | 20–26 min | **Mock Assertions for Integration Tests** | Use `pytest-mock`'s `mocker` fixture to assert that key functions were called with the expected arguments. These lightweight integration tests let you verify behavior without relying on external systems.
🔍 *Demo: Patch a service call and use `assert_called_once_with` and other functions to validate the interaction* | | 26–30 min | **Wrap-Up + Q\&A** | Recap main takeaways. Invite questions about testing challenges in real-life team environments. |
What motivates you to submit this propos: I would like to raise the awareness of the audience of how to write good code by testing it adequetly. Also there are only few talks on Pytest. I hope my talk can provide more perspective in this field.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: How to write good tests are often neglected in Python. While new technologies like AI and Data are becoming a hot topic, I would like to raise the audience's awareness about the basics of how to write good software and become a reliable Python developer -- the most important quality of a software engineer of whatever field. Furthermore, a lot of tutorials or talks on Pytest / other testing frameworks focus on the basics of Pytest, which doesn't consider much from a real-world perspective.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will gain invaluable skills on test suite speedup, advanced regression catching techniques and a new mental model on designing more testable code. These encourages audience to write tests and ship production with confidence.

Abstract:

Proposal title: Building Agentic AI on AWS: From Concept to Python Implementation
Abstract:
This presentation explores the rapidly evolving field of Agentic AI that is gaining significant industry attention, with a focus on practical Python-based implementations. 

The first section introduces the fundamental concepts and technical architecture of Agentic AI, Agentic IDE (Kiro), AgentCore, and MCP. 

The second section demonstrates concrete applications of Agentic AI on AWS built with Python, featuring a conversational weather agent implemented using Nova Act and Python libraries, alongside analyses of agent-based solutions for e-commerce and hotel reservation systems. 

The third section provides practical guidance on developing enterprise-grade Agentic AI applications using the open-source Strands Agents SDK with Python. 

This presentation aims to inspire innovative approaches among Python developers and foster collaborative exploration of the expanding potential in Python-based Agentic AI application development.
What motivates you to submit this propos: Agentic AI Development
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Agentic AI is the future
What value will the audience gain?: This presentation aims to inspire innovative approaches among Python developers and collectively explore the expanding frontiers of agent technology.

That's where Apify and Large Language Models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, come into play. Imagine being able to grab and organize web data easily, helping companies like Intercom get the info they need without the headache.

Proposal title: Security by Script: Automating Compliance with Python
Abstract: Security and compliance often feel like blockers—but they don’t have to be. In this talk, we’ll explore how Python can automate DevSecOps tasks like scanning cloud configurations, checking for policy drift, validating secrets, and enforcing guardrails in CI/CD. Using real examples with tools like checkov, bandit, and custom scripts, we’ll show how to make security a default part of development, not a last-minute audit. Ideal for DevOps engineers and SREs looking to build trust without slowing down delivery.
What motivates you to submit this propos: Having been responsible for both uptime and security posture, I know the tension between shipping fast and staying secure. I’ve used Python to bridge that gap with lightweight automation that adds guardrails without adding bureaucracy. I want to share that experience to help others bring compliance and development closer together.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is already a top choice for automation—but it’s underused in the security and compliance space. This talk shows the Python community how to use familiar tools to solve real-world security challenges, reducing friction between dev, ops, and compliance teams.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will learn how to use Python to automate common security checks, integrate them into pipelines, and reduce human error. They’ll leave with working examples, open-source tools, and patterns they can immediately apply to improve security without slowing down development.

Proposal title: How I Use Evals to Keep My AI Apps From Falling Apart
Abstract: As Large Language Model apps become more powerful and widely used, one challenge keeps surfacing: how do we know if they’re actually working well? LLM apps often fail silently with hallucinations, bugs, and inconsistent outputs going unnoticed. Manual reviews don’t scale. This talk introduces a practical 3-part evaluation framework using code checks, golden sets, and LLMs as judges to catch failures early, improve output quality, and help you build more reliable AI applications.
Description:
Most of us who build LLM-powered apps chatbots, summarizers, RAG pipelines know the pattern: you test a handful of prompts, everything looks fine, you ship… and then real users uncover off-topic answers, hallucinations, or odd formatting. Worse, there’s no reliable way to spot these issues early or track quality over time.

That’s where evaluations, or “evals,” come in. This talk presents a practical, iterative framework inspired by OpenAI’s internal approach and guided by one mantra, stop guessing, start testing. We’ll cover three layers of evals:

1. Code-based tests to catch structural mistakes wrong length, missing fields, bad JSON.

2. Golden sets of hand-checked responses to anchor accuracy and tone.

3. LLM-as-judge scoring that lets a larger model grade nuanced traits like fluency, helpfulness, and style.

A real-world case study will show how a six-step workflow identify failures, design evals, build datasets, generate, score, refine—tightened prompts and boosted quality. We’ll also explore building a trustworthy LLM judge through metaprompting and share tips for wiring these evals into CI pipelines. You’ll leave with a copy-pasteable playbook for testing your own LLM apps no massive datasets or deep ML expertise required, just a thoughtful setup and a bit of iteration.
Notes:
Prerequisites:
Intermediate Python skills (can follow functions and use assert)
Familiarity with LLM tools like GPT, LangChain, or similar
Interest in making your AI app more reliable and user-friendly
What motivates you to submit this propos: I chose this topic because in my nearly two years of working with Generative AI, I’ve seen how LLM apps can look great during testing but often fail when real users start using them. Things like hallucinations, bad formatting, or off-topic answers show up, and it's hard to catch them without a proper system. Learning how to use evals changed the way I build and test my apps it gave me a clear way to find issues early and improve quality. I want to share this with others so they can build more reliable AI apps without guessing or struggling.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: This topic is important to the Python community because many people are using Python to build AI apps, but it's not always easy to make sure those apps work well. In this talk, I’ll show how using evals (evaluation methods) can help you catch problems early, improve results, and build AI apps that people can trust. Even if someone is new to evals, they’ll leave with simple steps, useful tools, and ready-to-use ideas they can apply right away in their Python projects.

Proposal title: Before it Breaks: the Art of Managing Live sites
Abstract: Managing live sites is an annoying but necessary aspect of any large-scale software engineering system. Live sites come into the picture mainly because of four reasons: the software engineering system being imperfect, limitations regarding computing resources, difficulty in predicting user behavior, and interconnectedness with external service providers (in which case the live site is an inheritance). The proposed talk explores these four reasons, outlines ways to minimize the occurrence of live sites, and discusses strategies to address them effectively. Besides, it also delves into how a live site can teach us lessons that eventually help improve the system health in the long-term.
Notes:
Outline of the talk (total ~30 mins)

1. Introduction (3 min)
- What is a live site? 
- Common characteristics : urgency, user impact, varying levels of severity, etc. 

2. Why Live Sites get triggered? (4 mins)

Live sites usually get triggered because of four reasons. I plan to discuss them in details. 

- Software Engineering system being imperfect 
- Computing resources being finite
- The challenge in predicting user behavior
- External platform and resource dependencies ( for example, AWS outage impacting an e-commerce portal)

3. Small Case Study ( CrowdStrike incident July 2024) - 3 mins
- Details on its global impact
- What caused it and key take aways

3. Livesite Prevention Tactics (5 mins)
- Avoid single points of failure
- Prepare for the worst
- Document processes and recovery plans
- Automation of action items for recurring issues

4. During the Incident (6 min)
- Stop the bleeding (stabilize first)
- Prioritize, Act early 
- Seek help from an expert on the issue (if required)

5. Aftermath & Learning (4 min)
- Blameless post-mortems
- Analyze and fix the root cause
- Update documentation
- Live site as an opportunity to improve the system

6. Final remarks and Q/A (5 mins)
What motivates you to submit this propos: I am a Software Engineer dealing with live sites on a regular basis. I thought the lessons I learnt as a part of my Engineering responsibility would be helpful to other attendees. This motivated to submit the proposal.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Although this is not directly related to Python programming, the talk will be informative for programmers writing code in Python and building a large scale Software Engineering system.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will gain knowledge on the best practices on managing and mitigating live sites.

Proposal title: Building Real-World Multimodal AI Agents
Abstract:
Have you ever checked the ingredients list on a product while shopping at a mall?
If yes, you know the struggle—Googling each unknown keyword individually, switching between tabs, trying to make sense of chemical-sounding names.
Now imagine this:
You point your camera at a product, and an AI agent analyzes the image, understands the ingredients, performs a real-time web search, and gives you a clear, concise report—instantly.
Sounds amazing, right?
Well, that’s exactly what we’re going to build in this workshop.
Welcome to the world of multimodal AI agents, powered by Phidata and Gemini 2.0 Flash.
So next time you're at a supermarket, confused by a label —
Don’t Google 20 ingredients. Just click, analyze, and done! Let’s dive in and build something amazing!
Description:
Why Multimodal AI?
You might be wondering: “Why is multimodal AI such a big deal?”
Let me give you three real-world examples from my own experience:
1. Filling out Online Forms
You’re completing a government form, and suddenly you see a field labeled with some legal jargon. You have no idea what it means.
Solution:
Take a screenshot, upload it to a multimodal AI like Gemini, and ask:
“What does this field mean, and how should I fill it?”
The AI reads the image, understands the context, and helps you out.
2. Shopping at a Supermarket
You find a product with 12 unpronounceable ingredients. Instead of Googling each one:
Solution:
Click a photo, and let the AI analyze the ingredients and give health insights — all in one go.
3. Studying Diagrams for Exams
You're a student trying to understand a complex diagram from your textbook.
Solution:
Upload the image to a vision-language model like Gemini and ask:
“Explain this diagram like I’m 12.”
Boom — instant clarity.
So, What Are We Building?
In this workshop, we’ll build a product ingredients analyzer using:
1) Image input (upload or camera)
2)Gemini 2.0 Flash to understand images
3)Tavily to perform contextual web search
4)Custom system prompts to guide the AI’s role
5)Streamlit for a slick web interface
6)Phidata to orchestrate it all

Architecture Overview
The agent has 4 core parts:
LLM model – Gemini 2.0 Flash (for image understanding)
Tool – Tavily (for contextual web search)
System Prompt – to define the AI’s role
Instructions – to tell it how to respond
All these are stitched together with Phidata, and the UI is built using Streamlit.
Live Demo: How It Works
We’ll walk through two methods of providing images:
Method 1: Local image file path
Method 2: Public image URL
Example:
Upload an image of a shampoo bottle → AI extracts ingredients → performs web search for context → generates a markdown health report.
And it’s smart enough to not respond when it detects irrelevant inputs. For example, if you upload a photo of Messi (the footballer), it will say:
“This isn’t a product image. Please upload a product with ingredients.”
Now that’s responsible role-playing by the AI.
After testing everything locally, we’ll package it into a Streamlit app. Here’s what it includes:
1)Upload and capture image options
2)Realtime AI analysis (with streaming)
3)Clear markdown output (overview, nutrition facts, potential risks)
You can even deploy it live using Streamlit Cloud, add your API keys as secrets, and share the app with friends, colleagues, or even your nutritionist!
Bonus: Smart Prompts
We’ll also define a system prompt like:
"You are a food product analyst specialized in nutrition. Read the product ingredients, perform web search for unknown terms, and provide a health summary in markdown format."
This ensures the agent: Plays a consistent role, Uses web search only when needed and Writes clean, structured output.

By the end of this workshop, you’ll have a fully functional multimodal AI agent that can analyze products in real-time — and you’ll understand how to build similar agents for other use cases too.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I’m deeply motivated by the growing power of multimodal AI and its potential to solve everyday problems — not just for researchers or developers, but for anyone with a phone and a question. I’ve
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Multimodal AI is still underexplored in practical, workshop-friendly settings. This topic introduces Python developers to real-world, vision-language applications that are achievable using tools they already know or can quickly pick up. It’s an opportunity to expand the Python community’s reach into a future where language meets vision, grounded in real user needs.
What value will the audience gain?:
A hands-on understanding of how to build a multimodal AI application from scratch.

Exposure to cutting-edge tools like Gemini 2.0 Flash and Tavily, and how to integrate them.

Skills in prompt engineering to guide AI behavior reliably and responsibly.

A ready-to-deploy Streamlit app they can share or build on.

A clear blueprint for extending the architecture to other domains (education, accessibility, health tech, etc.).

Proposal title: pip install community
Abstract:
We learn Python through tutorials, bootcamps, or classes. Syntax here, libraries there. Maybe a few YouTube deep dives and some late-night Stack Overflow scrolling. The resources are endless.
But here’s what many miss: Python isn’t just a language. It’s a living, breathing community. And knowing that changes everything.
In this talk, we’ll look at the part of Python that doesn’t come in a package: its people. You’ll learn what the Python Software Foundation actually does (besides existing), how decisions about the language are made, and why even local meetups in Hong Kong are part of something much bigger.
Whether you’re new to Python, teaching it, or wondering what keeps this language thriving across the world—this talk will give you new ways to connect, contribute, and grow.
Because “Come for the language, stay for the community” isn’t just a feel-good line. It’s Python’s secret sauce. And once you taste it, it’s better than Lee Kum Kee.
What motivates you to submit this propos: To reach out to the local communities and talk more about the global structure of the Python.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Many people still have no idea what the Python Software Foundation is about and how language decisions are made.
What value will the audience gain?: Gain knowledge on the Python Software Foundation, the global community and how their contributions can help.

Proposal title: Python for the Paranoid: how to secure your Python code
Abstract: Vibe coding is great when it works, but less so when it leads to security vulnerabilities. This beginner-friendly introduction will equip you with the knowledge to make your Python code more secure. We will explore common ways Python projects can become susceptible to issues—from dependency risks to malicious data—and provide practical, actionable recommendations on tools and strategies to safeguard your work. Leave feeling more confident and less paranoid about your code.
Description:
## Motivation 

As a cybersecurity professional, I want to raise awareness of known Python security concerns in an easy-to-understand manner, especially for those who are new to the language. Intermediate-level learners are also welcome, if they wish to refresh their memory.

Especially in this era of “vibe coding”, I feel there is an overemphasis on “what works”, and a lack of consideration of “what might go wrong”. I hope this talk will inspire listeners to start coding with good cybersecurity hygiene. 

## Scope

This talk will cover security considerations unique to Python. This means that, instead of touching on general concepts like SQL injection or hardcoding secrets, I will focus on known security concerns and considerations in the Python ecosystem. 

## Talk outline

### Breakdown of why your code might be unsafe (20min)
1. Unsafe data (XML, zip, pickle)
2. Unsafe algorithms (random, hashlib)
3. Unsafe versions (using deprecated Python versions)
4. Unsafe third-party packages (supply chain attack)

In this section, to demonstrate the relevance and danger of these cases, I will supply real-life examples and easy-to-understand sample code. I will also recommend safer equivalents where available.

### Mitigation strategies (10min)

I will recommend some tools to address these concerns. In this age where the bulk of codebase may be generated by an AI tool, I will focus on tools that can be set up for automatic scans.

## References

Official list of modules with security considerations: https://docs.python.org/3/library/security_warnings.html  
Example of the ruff linter detecting dangerous pickle use: https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/suspicious-pickle-usage/
What motivates you to submit this propos:
As a cybersecurity professional, I want to raise awareness of known Python security concerns in an easy-to-understand manner, especially for those who are new to the language. Intermediate-level learners are also welcome, if they wish to refresh their memory.

Especially in this era of “vibe coding”, I feel there is an overemphasis on “what works”, and a lack of consideration of “what might go wrong”. I hope this talk will inspire listeners to start coding with good cybersecurity hygiene.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth:
Security concepts are often seen as something obscure or difficult. I want to show the relevance of these risks and prepare the community with the right knowledge and tools to secure their Python projects. 

I also want to put the spotlight on Python-specific security risks found in Python modules and the wider ecosystem.
What value will the audience gain?: Understand the different ways in which Python projects can turn out unsafe, in a context specific to the Python ecosystem and along with real-life examples. After my talk, the audience should be aware of practical tools they can employ to defend themselves against those risks.

Proposal title: Functional Python: Practical Paradigms for Readable and Robust Code
Abstract: While Python's object-oriented paradigm dominates developer discussions, its functional capabilities offer powerful tools for modern development. This talk explores how integrating functional programming (FP) concepts can enhance code readability and maintainability in Python projects. We will discover how to transform imperative logic flow into composable functions and implement declarative error-handling using intuitive railway patterns. This talk aims to provide an optional toolbox for Python developers to improve code quality.
Description:
Functional programming (FP) offers powerful tools and is increasingly adopted across modern languages, including Python. Since Python is not a purely functional language, rather than advocating for a complete shift to FP, this talk will demonstrate how to effectively integrate functional techniques, such as pure functions and higher-order functions, into your Python codebase. By converting imperative procedure-style logic into composable functions, developers can focus more on the "what" (logic) rather than the "how" (implementation details). As for error handling, we will explore how to organize code using a fun and easy-to-understand railway analogy. By the end of this talk, you'll understand how to apply basic FP concepts in Python, which improve code's readability, maintainability, and robustness.
The slides of this talk is available at [https://lucajiang.github.io/functional_python/](https://lucajiang.github.io/functional_python/)
Notes:
For intermediate Python developers familiar with OOP and basic FP concepts. No prior FP experience required, but familiarity with Python's functional features (like `map`, `filter`, and `lambda`) is helpful.

Although I applied for a 15-minute talk, I am open to a 30-minute slot if available. This would allow for a more in-depth exploration of functional programming techniques and their practical applications in Python.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I think the Python code should be simple and elegant. FP offers ways to achieve my expectations. I have been applying FP in R language and Rust (where FP is a more common practice) for a long time, and I find it really helpful. Also, I noticed some PEPs in recent Python versions have mentioned FP concepts. Therefore, I'd like to share my passion for FP with the Python community and demonstrate how it can enhance code quality in Python projects.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: FP is increasingly affecting modern software development, not only in functional languages but also in multi-paradigm languages like Python or Rust. Proposal title: Intuitive Jargon-Free Mental Model for MCP
Abstract:
You've heard about MCP (Model Context Protocol) and might have even used it. But after reading the specs and docs, you're still wondering: "Why can't I just use HTTP calls?" or "Why can't I just tell the LLM what commands to run?". I had these same questions until my two "aha" moments.
We all have those moments when learning something new, where everything clicks and makes sense. In this talk, I'll share the two "aha" moments that made MCP click for me. First, through a simple browser analogy that will make you wonder why nobody explained it this way before. Second, by revealing what MCP actually does to your prompts behind the scenes. My promise is that you will get to your aha moment and leave with an intuitive mental model of MCP.
Description:
Outline:

1. Introduction (2 mins): Who am I? Demo of what can be done by using GitHub MCP.
2. What are tools and why do LLMs need them? (2 mins)
3. The Browser Analogy That Changes Everything (3 mins): Analogy with familiar concepts (browsers and HTTP) to create an intuitive and jargon-free mental model that makes MCP obvious. Core insight #1 from the talk. Browsers <-HTTP-> Websites :: LLM applications <-MCP-> Tools. Just like web browser developers don't dictate what websites you can and can't visit, MCP helps users instead of LLM application developers to dictate what tools they can use.
4. Core Architecture (2 mins): Host, Client, and Server
5. The Magic of the MCP Client (3 mins): What MCP client really does? Example showing how the MCP client is basically injecting available tools in the system prompt behind the scenes. Core insight #2 from the talk.
6. A Minimal MCP Server in Python (5 mins)
7. The Full Tool-Call Timeline (3 mins): Step by step explanation starting from the point where LLM application starts and then user sends a prompt until the user receives the response 
8. Use MCP or Just Put Everything in the Prompt? (3 mins): What use cases are suitable for MCP? When you're better of putting all the necessary information in the prompt itself and making a single LLM call?
9. Security Concerns and Principal of Least Privilege (3 mins)
10. Conclusion (1 min)
11. Q&A (3 mins)

Audience:
Python developers interested in building or integrating with LLM applications, who may have heard of and even used MCP but want a clear, intuitive understanding of its purpose and basic mechanics.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I struggled with the official explanations for MCP for a long time. They felt abstract and didn't answer my fundamental questions like "Why is this better than just making an HTTP call?". After developing my own mental model that finally made the protocol "click", I wanted to share it the community. My motivation is to provide the community with the intuitive, jargon-free explanation I wish I had when I started.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is a dominant language for building LLM applications. To increase the capabilities of these applications, developers need standardized ways for models to interact with external tools. MCP is an emerging protocol designed for this purpose. An intuitive understanding of MCP helps developers build more capable applications and allows end-users to better understand and utilize them.
What value will the audience gain?:
- An intuitive and jargon-free mental model of MCP
- Ability to implement a minimal MCP server in Python
- Criteria for deciding when to adopt MCP in your own projects

Proposal title: High Dimensions, Low Hassle: Solving the Curse with Python
Abstract: High-dimensional datasets are common in modern data science workflows but they come at a cost. From bloated training times to overfitting and inscrutable patterns, the “curse of dimensionality” can quietly sabotage even the most promising machine learning projects. In this session, we'll demystify what this curse really is, why it matters, and how you can break free from it using Python. Through visual examples and practical code, we’ll explore dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and autoencoders. You'll see how these methods simplify data while preserving structure, improve model performance, and reveal hidden insights that are otherwise lost in the noise. Whether you're a beginner aiming to better understand high-dimensional data, or an experienced practitioner looking to optimize and interpret complex datasets, this talk will give you practical tools to make your models faster, cleaner, and smarter.
Description:
High-dimensional data is increasingly common in modern data science, but it often introduces more complexity than value. With too many features, models become slower to train, more prone to overfitting, and harder to interpret. In this talk, we’ll explore practical strategies to manage and simplify high-dimensional datasets, tackling what’s known as the “curse of dimensionality.” We'll begin by unpacking this curse explaining why high-dimensional spaces can lead to sparse data, distorted distance measures, and misleading patterns that reduce the effectiveness of machine learning models. This foundational understanding will set the stage for discussing how to address these challenges through dimensionality reduction.

We’ll dive into some of the most widely used dimensionality reduction techniques in Python, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and neural network–based autoencoders. Each method will be introduced with its strengths, limitations, and ideal use cases. Through clear, concise code examples using libraries like scikit-learn, umap-learn, and keras, you’ll see how these techniques reduce data complexity while preserving the underlying structure.

A key focus will be on how dimensionality reduction improves model efficiency reducing training time, simplifying hyperparameter tuning, and enhancing generalization by removing noise and redundancy. We'll also look at how it can aid data exploration, with visual examples that show how reducing dimensions helps uncover hidden patterns and relationships that are hard to detect in raw feature spaces.

The session concludes with real-world applications, offering tips on how to incorporate dimensionality reduction into your own data pipelines. Whether you're just starting with machine learning or looking to refine existing workflows, this talk will provide actionable insights to help you better manage complex datasets and build more robust, interpretable models.

Proposal title: Setting Up Reliable CI/CD Pipelines with Python, K8s & Testcontainers
Abstract: Build a production-grade CI/CD pipeline using Python, Docker, Testcontainers, GitHub Actions, and Kubernetes. This workshop takes you from zero to deployment with real-world automation, testing, and monitoring. Perfect for all levels, it blends simplicity, storytelling, and powerful DevOps tools to boost your confidence in delivering reliable software.
Description:
Shipping software should feel empowering — not like fighting fires. Yet for many developers, CI/CD feels like a maze of YAMLs, fragile tests, cloud complexity, and guesswork. This workshop changes that story, using Python as your guiding light.

In this 85-minute hands-on session, you’ll build a complete, production-grade CI/CD pipeline — one that starts with a commit and ends with a deployed, monitored app in the cloud. But unlike most DevOps sessions, this one is crafted through the lens of simplicity, storytelling, and the power of Python.

We'll start with Python scripts that automate GitHub repo creation and Jenkins setup. From there, you’ll use Testcontainers to run realistic integration tests in Docker — giving you confidence that your tests reflect the real world. We'll automate builds and trigger workflows using GitHub Actions, then containerize your app and push it to Docker Hub.

Then comes the moment of truth: deploying your Python app to a live Kubernetes cluster (AWS EKS), using Python to manage manifests, rollouts, and environment configs. To top it off, you'll integrate a custom Prometheus exporter written in Python, visualized in Grafana, so you can watch your app breathe in real time.

This isn’t just another workshop filled with configs. It’s a journey — from chaos to clarity, from “I’m not sure what I’m doing” to “I actually built that!” Every step is hands-on, beginner-friendly, and deeply practical. We blend technical depth with real-world insight, humour, and moments of celebration.

Whether you’re just starting out with DevOps, or you’re a seasoned engineer who wants a clean, Pythonic approach to CI/CD, this session is for you. You’ll leave with a complete working pipeline, a solid understanding of every tool involved, and the confidence to recreate it at work, in your side projects, or with your teams.

By the end, you’ll walk away not only with skills, but with a story — a story of how you connected the dots and built something amazing, powered by Python.

Proposal title: Retain the Insight, not the Data: KPI engineering with Python when pieces are missing
Abstract:
In today’s AI-powered data-driven world, respecting user privacy choices is more critical than ever, and data teams are increasingly asked to delete sensitive user information from their systems and Data Warehouses upon request. For Data and Analytics Engineering, this presents the challenge to maintain business metrics reliable and stable along with the evolution of AI, machine learning and business analysis.
My goal is to empower the community to use python-driven processes to ensure AI and analytics efforts remain productive and reliable, minimizing the frustration and misalignment between business expectations and data realities. I want to help others avoid common pitfalls and contribute to a community where user privacy is seen as a core value.
Description:
This talk will reflect how diverse pieces -privacy constraints, analytical logic, data pipelines, and Python tooling- come together in resilient, privacy-respecting analytics systems, with practical insights into assembling a strong foundation for data-driven environments.

What happens when some of the data used to build your KPIs is no longer available?
How do you ensure the continuity, comparability, and integrity of business metrics when foundational data is missing?

We’ll explore a Python-driven stack, combining modular tooling, layered data modeling, and observability practices that enables us to “keep the insight” even after “losing the data”.

The audience will learn:
- How to architect a system to recompute metrics with partial raw data.
- How to balance privacy and business needs, using Python-based tools like attrs-based classes, enumerations, objects, jinja templates, yaml schemas and a custom observability logic.
- Create fallback data representations e.g. metric-only tables, anonymized metrics.
- Lessons learned from treating metric systems as living, fault-tolerant entities.
Notes:
As a staff data engineer working on privacy-first strategies for years, I've attended PyCon sessions mostly focused on data collection or storage.
This talk offers an innovative analytics engineering perspective as it explores a seldom-addressed frontier: how to preserve business insight when underlying data is no longer available due to deletion, summarization, or regulatory constraints, an emerging challenge in privacy-first and compliance-bound environments.

What value will the audience gain?:

Proposal title: Building a Production-Ready MCP Server with Agentic Workflows, Vector DBs, and Streaming in Python
Abstract:
Modern AI applications demand seamless integration between large language models, persistent knowledge stores, and responsive user interactions. In this talk, I’ll guide you through building a robust MCP (Model-Client-Protocol) server in Python that supports environment-based configuration, secure API key management, vector database integration using Quadrant, and token-streaming responses with Server-Sent Events (SSE).

We’ll explore how to orchestrate agentic workflows using Agno, connect advanced language models like Gemini 2.5, and implement custom MCP tools for web search and video retrieval. Through a step-by-step walkthrough with code examples, you’ll see how to manage asynchronous client-server communication, handle embeddings with Fast Embed, and save/retrieve data efficiently from a vector DB.

Whether you’re building chatbots, knowledge assistants, or AI agents, this talk offers practical patterns and reusable components for scalable, maintainable AI services—all built in Python.
Description:
In this hands-on workshop, you will learn how to build a fully functional MCP (Model-Client-Protocol) server in Python that supports environment-based configuration and advanced AI workflows. Starting from the basics, we will cover how to connect your MCP server with environment variables for secure API key management, integrate a vector database (Quadrant) to persist useful responses as embeddings, and leverage sentence transformers to efficiently save and retrieve information.

The workshop will also demonstrate how to implement Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming token-by-token model responses, enabling responsive and real-time client-server communication. You will build an agentic workflow using Agno as the orchestrator and Gemini 2.5 as the language model, while defining custom MCP tools for web and video search to enrich your AI assistant.

By the end of this session, you’ll have a deep understanding of:

How to configure MCP servers with environment variables and vector databases

Creating agentic workflows with custom tools and LLM integration

Implementing streaming communication via SSE for real-time responses
Notes: This workshop is ideal for Python developers and AI practitioners eager to build scalable, maintainable, and production-ready AI assistant backends using modern open-source tools.
What motivates you to submit this propos: This workshop teaches participants how to build a scalable, maintainable MCP (Model-Client-Protocol) server backend for AI assistants using Python. We will cover environment-based configuration for secure API key management, integrating vector databases (Quadrant) for persistent knowledge storage, and leveraging agentic workflows with Agno and Gemini 2.5 language models. Additionally, attendees will implement real-time streaming responses using Server-Sent Events (SSE) to enable responsive AI applications. Practical coding demos and best practices for async Python in AI workflows will be highlighted.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: This workshop is ideal for Python developers, AI engineers, and practitioners who want to build production-ready AI assistant backends. Prior Python experience is recommended, as well as some familiarity with asynchronous programming and large language models, but no advanced knowledge is required. Attendees eager to learn about open-source tools for AI orchestration, vector databases, and real-time streaming will find this especially valuable.
What value will the audience gain?:
Configure and deploy MCP servers with environment variables for secure API key management.

Integrate vector databases to store and retrieve AI-generated knowledge using text embeddings.

Build and orchestrate agentic workflows with custom tools using Agno and Gemini 2.5 LLM.

Implement Server-Sent Events (SSE) to stream AI responses token-by-token for real-time interaction.

Write efficient asynchronous Python code for AI applications and handle common pitfalls in event loops.

Proposal title: Supercharge Your AI with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google ADK
Abstract:
What if you could take your AI from just chatting and writing to actually doing stuff? Like, real-world tasks. Well, buckle up because the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is here to turn your language models into action heroes! In this talk, we’ll dive deep into the magic of MCP, the secret sauce that lets Claude, Gemini 2.5, and other LLMs communicate with tools, APIs, and external systems.
Imagine this: Your AI isn’t just answering questions— it is saving files, querying databases, and running real tasks. That’s the power of MCP. By the end of this session, you’ll not only understand how MCP works but also how to make your AI systems powerful by giving them real-world action abilities.
You’ll learn:
* Why LLMs like Claude and Gemini 2.5 need a little help to do real-world stuff.
* How MCP acts as a translator, letting your AI talk to tools like vector DBs and APIs
* How to combine Google ADK + MCP to build action-ready AI agents
* And yep, a live demo!
Description:
This is where the fun begins! We’re going to break it down and level up your AI game by exploring how MCP transforms your language model into a world-action hero. Here’s how we’re doing it:
1. Why LLMs Need Some Help:
* LLMs like Claude and Gemini 2.5 are amazing at generating content, but when it comes to actually doing something (like querying a database or calling an API), they hit a wall. This is where MCP comes in. We’ll show you how it gives these models the power to take action and interact with the real world.
2. MCP Architecture – The Backstage Pass:
* Let’s peel back the curtain on the MCP architecture and look at the four main pieces of the puzzle: tools (external services), decision-making (LLMs doing the heavy thinking), memory (keeping track of everything in an in-memory session), and execution (running the tasks asynchronously without a hitch). We’ll go through how these components all work together to create a super-efficient agent.
3. Integrating Google ADK and MCP:
* Ready to make your AI even cooler? We’ll walk you through the process of getting Google ADK up and running with MCP. You’ll learn how to integrate your LLM with MCP servers so your AI can do things like fetch live listings or store/retrieve data. All it takes is a little bit of config and you’ve got yourself an agent that does stuff.
4. Live Demo: The Cool Part:
* Let’s get our hands dirty. In this part, we’ll walk through a live demo where we’ll set up an agent to query Airbnb listings in Paris (because, why not?). You’ll see how easy it is to set up an agent, define the right tools, and have the agent bring back real-time data in response to a user query. Trust me, it’s cooler than it sounds.
This is not your average technical talk. If you want to take your AI skills from passive to action-packed, this session will show you exactly how to build intelligent agents that can do stuff. We’ll take you from theory to real-world action with hands-on examples and a live demo that’ll leave you excited to try this out in your own projects. Get ready to supercharge your AI, and trust me — it’s going to be a fun ride.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I submitted this proposal because I believe we’re at a turning point in how we use LLMs — moving from passive assistants to active agents that do things. Too many developers are still treating LLMs like smart autocomplete. This session is about showing what’s possible when you give your LLMs the power to interact with the real world — calling APIs, fetching real-time data, and making decisions. I’ve had a blast building with MCP, and I want to help others break through the same limitations I faced early on. If we can make AI that acts, not just chats, we unlock a whole new category of applications.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is the de facto language of AI, and it's also uniquely positioned to lead the charge into agent-based architectures. MCP (and similar orchestration tools) give Python developers the ability to build LLM-driven agents that interact with external services, automate workflows, and actually get things done — all in a Pythonic way. The Python community is full of builders, and this topic gives them the tools and mindset shift to move beyond traditional prompts and toward action-oriented AI. It’s not just the next step for LLMs — it’s the next step for Python developers in AI.
What value will the audience gain?:
Audience members will walk away with:

A working understanding of how to design LLM agents that perform real-world actions.

Hands-on experience integrating external tools and APIs via MCP.

A clear mental model for the architecture behind autonomous, memory-aware agents.

Practical skills they can immediately use to build smarter, more useful AI tools.

And most importantly — confidence to go beyond ChatGPT clones and build truly interactive apps.

Proposal title: OCR is Dead? Transcribing Images with LLMs
Abstract: Can modern Large Language Models outperform traditional OCR tools in real-world tasks like CAPTCHA solving, handwritten notes, or scanned PDFs? This talk compares traditional OCR techniques with vision-enabled LLMs using Python. Through hands-on examples, such as CAPTCHAs, handwriting, and complex PDFs, we’ll explore what works, what doesn’t, and where LLMs shine.
Description:
Text extraction from images isn’t what it used to be. For years, OCR tools like Tesseract, EasyOCR, or PaddleOCR have been the go-to solution. But now, with vision-capable LLMs like Mistral OCR and other multimodal models, we can read the text and understand its meaning.

In this talk, I’ll demonstrate several real-world tasks where Python developers often need to extract or understand text from visual inputs:

- CAPTCHA solving: comparing OCR vs LLM approaches to bypass distorted or obfuscated text
- Single-page documents: dealing with scanned documents, noise, layout issues
- Handwritten text recognition: limitations of OCR and how LLMs generalize better
- PDFs: reading multi-column, rotated, or annotated PDFs with both tools

I'll compare each use case side by side with Python code, using libraries like pytesseract, pdfplumber, PaddleOCR, and API-based LLMs like GPT-4 Vision. We’ll explore accuracy, flexibility, cost, latency, and Python-friendliness.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I’ve been experimenting with both OCR libraries and LLMs in real-world tasks, and I’ve been amazed (and surprised) at what works and what doesn’t. I want to share what I’ve learned so others don’t have to go through the same trial-and-error.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: A lot of people still default to old OCR tools without realizing how far things have come. Python is central to both the classic and modern approaches, and this topic bridges both worlds.
What value will the audience gain?: Practical, working knowledge. They’ll walk away knowing when to use OCR, when to switch to LLMs, and how to do both in Python with actual code examples.

Proposal title: Learning Python in the age of AI
Abstract: The advent of AI tools, especially large language models (LLMs), has transformed how we learn and teach. This talk focuses mainly on the learning aspect, particularly how AI tools can support individuals beginning their programming journey. We will discuss about best practices to consider while using these tools such that they empower the learning process and not replace it.
Notes:
Outline of the talk ( total 15 mins) 

1. Beginning : I will start this talk with an example from book ( Brave New World, Salman Khan), in which a professor in 2023 ( during the early days of ChatGPT) discovered that using ChatGPT, the students in the class were cheating with their essay and how the professor changed the teaching style so that AI tools were rather integrated in his class, which ultimately benefitted the students. [ 2 mins] 

2. Then I will focus on the learning part. I will emphasize that this talk is specifically about "learning".  I will include a flow chart of a general learning process that explains the general steps of learning (base knowledge -> curiosity -> exploration -> practice -> mastery).  I will also share why learning Python or any other programming language is still essential even though LLMs help write code. [3 mins] 

3. Then I will explain where AI tools come into picture during the learning process. I will emphasize on these four things while using the tools for learning [3 mins] 
- Need to understand how the tools work 
- They are not right all the time
- They hallucinate. Always verify responses through reliable sources or through experimentation. 
- They also have their own biases

4. Best practices [3 mins] 
- Using an AI tool as an assistant and not a replacement of yourself
- Engage with continuous critical thinking. Using AI tools shouldn't stop the critical thinking. 
- Use the tools to outline steps for a new idea
- Speed up the learning process with context specific questions or using an AI tool as an individualized tutor

5. I will summarize the talk by encouraging participants to think about three questions ( cited from the book -- AI and the Future of Education, Pritam Shah). [2 mins] 
- What are the AI and machine learning, and what tools already exist ?
- How can I use AI to solve my problems?
- When might I choose to use or not use AI or a particular tool? 

I will also tie / circle back to the central idea of this talk that AI tools should empower learning and not replace it. 

6. Q/A : 2 mins
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: This topic will be interesting for audience who are starting their journey with Python or any other programming language. They will learn how they can use the AI tools and facilitate their learning process.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will learn to use AI tools in a more mindful way.

Proposal title: AI工具改變了Python甚麼 / How AI Tools Changed the Python Language
Abstract:
新興的AI工具，例如Github copilot和cursor，令寫程式更方便。但我發現這些工具俏俏地改變了Python這個語言，我會用幾個例子，預測未來Python這個語言的改變，我們可以做甚麼，以及為何這些改變會出現。

The new AI tools, such as GitHub Copilot or Cursor, have made programming easier. However, I observed that these tools silently changed the Python language. I will give a few examples to explain and predict the future of Python language. I will give my opinion on why this happens and what we can do about it.
Description:
一個語言並不限於語法，還有使用習慣，例如Microsoft喜歡用Hungarian notation寫C++。長久以來，Python都是以簡潔著稱，某程度上可能源於懶惰，所以type annotation和docstring的不見於所有程式。然而，AI工具的出現會令寫出這些「沒用的部件」更廉價，從而令之更盛行。另一方面，這些工具肯定令人少了思考，產出的語言更單一。我會用一些例題看看這些工具如何塑造Python的未來，以及解釋為何Python會比其他語言更容易受到AI工具的影響。
為配合比喻及笑話，這個講題會用廣東話，如觀眾要求配合，可即場改以英語進行。

A language is not only its syntax but also its conventions of usage. For example, Microsoft is famous for using Hungarian notation in C++.

Python is famous for its concise syntax. There are type annotations and docstrings in the language, but they are not used by all projects. This is partially because humans are too lazy to do this extra work. The availability of the AI tools will make these "useless bits" cheap to add and thus more common. On the other hand, AI outputs are more uniform, unoriginal, and dull. I will prove this with some examples. I will also explain why it is the case, why Python is more susceptible to these problems than other languages, and what we should do about it.

This talk is intended to be delivered in Cantonese because of the jokes and analogies, but it can be switched to English if the audiences prefer.
What motivates you to submit this propos: My recent experience in using AI tools at work.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Do you know? Python is the most common language among all source code in the dataset for training large language models.
What value will the audience gain?: I am telling what I see from my crystal ball about the future of the Python language

Proposal title: From Manual to Autonomous: Building AI Agents for Smarter QA with Python
Abstract:
In a world of fast-changing software, traditional testing is becoming outdated—slow, manual, and hard to scale. This workshop teaches you how to use Python + AI agents to create smarter, self-adapting test systems.

You’ll learn how to build an AI-powered test automation pipeline using LangChain, PyTest, and Selenium, where agents can plan, write, update, and verify test cases with little manual input. We’ll use LLMs like OpenAI or Ollama to understand requirements, generate test logic, and even detect bugs.

Key highlights:

Generate test cases using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Automate UI testing with agents that respond to code changes

Integrate ML/LLM models for bug detection

Build a full-stack QA workflow from scratch

Description:

How to turn product specs or UI flows into actionable, AI-generated tests

How agents can automatically update tests as your app evolves

How to use AI to analyze failed tests and pinpoint bugs

How to build reusable testing agents to scale QA across teams

By the end, you’ll have a working AI test pipeline, ready to plug into your projects. This workshop is ideal for QA engineers, SDETs, and Python developers excited to future-proof their testing using AI.
Notes: This workshop is a merge of three tightly connected topics: AI agent-driven testing, RAG-based test case generation, and end-to-end automation with LangChain and Selenium. I want to share my learnings to help others future-proof their QA processes and embrace the shift from manual to autonomous testing.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is at the heart of modern AI, automation, and testing frameworks. With the rise of LLMs and tools like LangChain, it's the perfect time for the Python community to adopt these technologies for smarter QA. This workshop bridges AI and testing using accessible, Python-native tools.

Proposal title: Peek Inside the Pixels: Visual Interpretability for Computer Vision Models
Abstract: As computer vision becomes more deeply integrated into real-world applications, understanding how and why models make decisions is no longer optional, it’s essential. This talk introduces practical interpretability techniques that bring transparency to computer vision models. We’ll explore popular methods such as Grad-CAM and LIME, and see how they reveal the inner workings of deep learning models through visual explanations. Through live demos, attendees will learn how these tools can be used to debug models, uncover biases, and build trust with users. Designed for Python developers of all backgrounds, this session makes a complex topic accessible even if you're new to machine learning or explainable AI.
Notes: In this session, we’ll dive into the world of interpretability for computer vision models, a crucial step toward building more transparent, reliable, and ethical AI systems. You’ll learn how techniques like Grad-CAM and LIME visually highlight what parts of an image a model is focusing on when making predictions. Through hands-on demos and real-world examples, we’ll explore how these tools help developers debug models, detect potential biases, and improve user trust. Whether you're a developer, researcher, or just curious about how AI “sees,” this talk will break down complex concepts into beginner-friendly insights you can apply in your own projects.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I wanted to share my passion for computer vision as it is now a less popular topic because of the rise of Generative AI.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: It can promote responsible AI development by helping developers understand and trust the behavior of computer vision models. As Python is the leading language in AI, equipping its practitioners with interpretability tools ensures more transparent and ethical applications.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will gain practical knowledge of interpretability techniques, with hands-on strategies to visualize and debug computer vision models. They’ll leave with a clearer understanding of how AI makes decisions and how to build more transparent and trustworthy systems using Python.

Proposal title: What’s Really Going On in Your Model? A Python Guide to Explainable AI
Abstract:
As machine learning models become more complex, understanding why they make certain predictions is becoming just as important as the predictions themselves. Whether you're dealing with business stakeholders, regulators, or just debugging unexpected results, the ability to explain your model is no longer optional , it's essential.

In this talk, we'll walk through practical tools in the Python ecosystem that help bring transparency to your models, including SHAP, LIME, and Captum. Through hands-on examples, you'll learn how to apply these libraries to real-world models from decision trees to deep neural networks and make sense of what's happening under the hood.

If you've ever struggled to explain your model’s output or justify its decisions, this session will give you a toolkit to build more trustworthy, interpretable systems  without sacrificing performance.
Description: We’ve all been there, your machine learning model performs well in testing, but when it comes time to explain why it made a specific prediction, things get murky. In many real-world applications, especially in domains like healthcare, finance, or operations, being able to explain your model isn’t just helpful it’s critical.This talk is a practical walkthrough of explainable AI (XAI) tools in Python, aimed at data scientists and engineers who want to make their models more transparent and trustworthy. We’ll cover libraries like SHAP, LIME, and Captum, and show how to use them to generate both local and global explanations for models ranging from random forests to deep neural nets.You’ll see hands-on examples, common pitfalls to avoid, and ideas for integrating interpretability into your workflow whether you’re trying to debug your model or justify its predictions to a non-technical stakeholder.If you’ve ever wanted to better understand your own models or help others trust them this session is for you.

Proposal title: SLIs, SLOs, and Python: A Love Story

In this talk, we’ll walk through how Python can bridge that gap by collecting SLIs from real systems, evaluating SLO compliance, and automating reporting. Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Reliability is no longer just an ops concern—it’s a shared responsibility, and Python is increasingly at the heart of the tools we use to measure and manage it. This topic shows how the Python community can contribute to and lead in reliability engineering practices like SLIs and SLOs. By using familiar libraries and Pythonic workflows, we can empower developers and SREs alike to build more observable, self-healing systems—bringing Dev and Ops closer together in true DevOps spirit.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will walk away with a practical understanding of SLIs and SLOs—what they are, why they matter, and how to implement them using Python. They'll see real-world examples of collecting metrics, evaluating reliability, and automating reports with Python tools they likely already know. Whether they’re SREs, developers, or DevOps engineers, attendees will gain actionable strategies to improve system reliability without needing expensive platforms—just smart use of Python and thoughtful design.

Proposal title: Observability Matters: Empowering Python Developers with OpenTelemetry.
Abstract:
Have you ever imagined your app crashing at the worst possible moment? Right when a user is about to check out or during some internal transaction that really matters? It happens. And when it does, users don’t wait. They leave. But behind that one crash is a bigger story: teams scrambling, dashboards lighting up, and no clear answer to why it failed. Systems today are too complex, distributed, fast-moving, and full of silent breakpoints. A single failure can ripple out fast. And when you’re in the middle of it, juggling multiple tools, good luck figuring out what caused it.

This talk sees observability not as an ops problem, but as an engineering discipline, one built on open standards like OpenTelemetry, that gives you control without locking you into yet another vendor. You’ll learn how to instrument Python code, process telemetry, and export it for analysis. It's not just about logs, metrics, or traces. It's about clarity. It’s about identifying why something unexpected happened. Whether you're a developer or someone who gets the call when things go down, this session is for you. Attendees will leave with practical knowledge on how to reduce their tradational observability cost on a bigger picture. Let's see observability as a shared responsibility across teams.
Description:
# Key topics:

- The evolution of observability and why it has become essential over the past few decades.

- A deep dive into core telemetry signals: Logs, Metrics, and Traces.

- The challenges developers face with modern observability, and how adopting OpenTelemetry can address these issues.

What motivates you to submit this propos:
Well, I'm not an OG but I’ve spent countless hours learning from and working alongside veterans of this field. So, I can definitely bet on this: I have a story worth sharing, shaped by my experiences, challenges, and breakthroughs over the years.

From beginning, Python has been at the heart of my development journey, and attending PyCon events worldwide has connected me with the vibrant and diverse developer community. This year, however, feels uniquely special. I’m not just learning; I’m contributing, sharing insights on a topic I’ve immersed myself in - how observability tools directly impact application performance and sustainability.

In 2022, I worked on a critical research project focused on observability. Our team faced a budget crunch that demanded creative solutions. That’s when I discovered OpenTelemetry. My journey with it began as a curious learner, evolved into open-source contributions, and recently culminated in helping design the CNCF certification for the OpenTelemetry Certified Associate. This hands-on experience has given me a nuanced understanding of the tool, its challenges, and its transformative potential.

Moreover, what sets this talk apart is its developer-centric perspective. While I’ve often spoken about OpenTelemetry in DevOps and platform contexts, this time, I’m speaking directly to developers, the people who feel the real impact when new tools are introduced and old ones are replaced. This talk is for you if you’ve no idea what exactly is observability or ever been handed a tool like OpenTelemetry with little context and told to “just integrate it.” 

I’m here to share what my team learned the hard way, where we failed, where we made progress, and what actually helped us adopt OpenTelemetry at scale in a way that made sense for engineering teams. Because this isn’t just about metrics or traces. It’s about helping developers build software that is faster, more reliable, and easier to understand. 

Observability, when approached the right way, becomes a powerful part of the software engineering process, not just an operations afterthought. And that’s the core of why I’m giving this talk. For too long, observability has been treated as a monitoring function for operators. But that view is limited. Operators use telemetry data to watch systems. 

Developers create the systems that generate that data, and we use it to debug, optimize, and design better software from the inside out. Observability isn’t an ops problem. It’s an engineering discipline. And when developers treat it that way, we can do more than just keep systems running, we can make them better.

I’ve spoken with around more than hundred people including Sr. SWE, TL, CTOs up to this year, and I’ve found that the majority of Python developers - whether at early-stage startups or Fortune 500 companies - rely heavily on old proprietary monitoring and observability solutions. That’s why I want to highlight open standards in the observability landscape using OpenTelemetry, which is the second most active Kubernetes project under the CNCF. It lets developers take control of their telemetry data, they decide what to send, where to send it, and how to send it. The vendor no longer decides for them. This empowers developers to build the next generation of applications.
