Proposal title: Mercari LLM Benchmark: Building a Practical LLM Benchmark for Your Business
Abstract: Every new LLM comes with glowing performance on English-centric benchmarks. This makes it difficult to predict how that performance will translate to business use cases in other languages or specialized domains. At Mercari, Japan's largest C2C marketplace, we faced this exact problem with Japanese. Inspired by Kagi, Wolfram, and Aider benchmarks, we are building our own continuously updated internal benchmark to evaluate major LLMs on unpolluted, business-critical tasks that models have not seen in their training data. The talk will cover task design, an evaluation pipeline in Python, a comparison of the latest models on accuracy, cost, and latency, and practical lessons for creating your own benchmark tailored to your needs.
Description:
Outline
1. Motivation: Why Standard Benchmarks Fail in Non-English Contexts. Speaker introduction. (2 minutes)
2. Task Taxonomy and Dataset Curation: Creating unpolluted tasks that mirror real business problems. Examples of tasks. (3 minutes)
3. Python Evaluation Pipeline: A robust, automated pipeline with Litellm, Pydantic, SQLite, etc. (9 minutes)
4. Methodology and Metrics: Ensuring fair, unpolluted evaluation beyond simple accuracy. (3 minutes)
5. Results: A snapshot of how the latest major LLMs perform on our private, business-critical tasks. (3 minutes)
6. Surprising Trade-offs: Analyzing the Pareto frontier of accuracy, cost, and speed for production systems. (3 minutes)
7.  Building Your Own Benchmark: Essential Python libraries, design patterns, and practical lessons. (5 minutes)
8. Conclusion and Q&A (2 minutes)

Audience
Python developers, ML/DS engineers, tech leads, and product managers using Large Language Models for real-world business applications, especially in non-English or specialized domains.
What motivates you to submit this propos: Public LLM benchmarks are English-centric and fail to predict performance on non-English business tasks (in our case Japanese). To make informed, data-driven decisions about which models to use in production, we are building our own practical, private benchmark. We chose this topic because many companies face this same problem, and our Python-based methodology provides a reusable blueprint for them.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is the primary language for AI/ML, and developers are increasingly integrating LLMs. Standard benchmarks are often English-centric and poor predictors of real-world performance. This talk provides a practical, Python-based blueprint for custom evaluation. It empowers developers to make data-driven decisions on model selection (accuracy, cost, latency) for their specific use cases and promoting robust engineering within the Python ecosystem.
What value will the audience gain?:
- Performance (accuracy, cost, latency, etc.) of the latest LLMs on real-world non-English (Japanese) business tasks.
- A blueprint for a Python-based evaluation pipeline for automated, robust, and multi-provider benchmarking.
- A step-by-step process to build your own small-scale, high-impact LLM benchmark tailored to your specific business problems.

This workshop helps the Python community by:

Exposure to best practices in monitoring distributed systems

Proposal title: Debugging LLM Pipelines in Python- Engineering Lessons from the Trenches
Abstract: LLMs are powerful but things can quickly go wrong when you’re building real apps. Prompts may fail, tool calls can break, and outputs often behave in unexpected ways. In this talk, we’ll look at real-world issues developers face when working with Python-based LLM pipelines and how to fix them. You’ll walk away with practical debugging tips and tools to help make your AI apps more stable and trustworthy.
Description:
This talk shares lessons learned from hands-on experience building LLM-powered applications using Python. We'll walk through the common problems that show up in the real world like broken toolchains, failing prompts, inconsistent responses, and unexpected agent behaviors.

The session focuses on practical debugging strategies: how to trace issues, log properly, test prompts like code, and use tools like langsmith or simple logs to spot problems early. We’ll also touch on memory management, retry logic, and why some issues only show up after your app goes live. Whether you're using LangChain, CrewAI, or your own pipeline logic, this talk will give you the mindset and techniques to debug faster, work smarter, and build more reliable AI systems.

No heavy theory just real engineering practices from the field.

# Outline:
0–3 mins: Setting the Stage
3–8 mins: What Goes Wrong in Real Projects
8–14 mins: Shift Your Mindset, LLMs Are Code, Not Magic
14–20 mins: Debugging in Practice Tools That Help
20–26 mins: Lessons That Made My Life Easier
26–30 mins: Final Thoughts + Q&A

# Key Takeaways
Know where and why LLM apps break in real workflows
Use open-source tools to debug prompts, agents, and memory
Apply versioning, logging, and testing strategies to prompt chains
Learn debugging practices that improve developer productivity
Notes:
# Prerequisites:
Basic to intermediate knowledge of Python
Familiarity with LLM concepts (e.g., prompts, context windows, API calls to models like GPT or Claude) Experience building or debugging any kind of pipeline doesn’t have to be GenAI-specific. 
Finally, interest to learn new things.
What motivates you to submit this propos: It’s been close to two years now that I’ve been working hands-on with GenAI projects  like building apps, fine-tuning models, and designing pipelines with tools like LangChain, CrewAI, and custom Python frameworks. One thing I’ve learned the hard way, even the smartest teams end up wasting hours chasing ghosts in their LLM pipelines. Not because they lack talent but because debugging LLM workflows is just different. And no, fancy tools alone won’t save you. What really matters is developing solid debugging habits early on. This talk is my way of sharing those lessons, so developers, AI engineers, data scientists and data folks feel more confident when things inevitably go wrong because they will.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will learn how to stop treating LLMs like unpredictable black boxes and start seeing them as systems you can understand and control. I’ll share a clear, practical approach to debugging issues so you don’t panic when something breaks. Whether you're using tools like LangChain, CrewAI, or your own custom setup, the same mindset and methods apply. Even if you're just getting started with GenAI, these lessons will give you a strong foundation to build and debug with confidence.

Proposal title: Pythonic Finance: Analyze Company Fundamentals with SEC EDGAR APIs
Abstract:
In this talk, Python and quantitative methods are used to access, validate, and analyze fundamental financial data from the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) EDGAR system. The SEC's JSON API provides structured financial data, derived from company filings reported in eXtensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL), an international standard for financial reporting. Pydantic is used for robust data validation. Attendees will learn to:

- Fetch basic metrics
- Calculate financial ratios
- Visualize trends
- Navigate common data challenges

While focused on the US market data, a brief explanation of the international landscape will also be provided. No finance background required. Basic Python is required to understand the data processing part.
Description:
### Target

- **Who**: This talk is designed for anyone interested in using Python to understand public company financials, spanning from students, programmers, hobbyists, even experienced working professionals. As mentioned, no finance background is required for this talk. Beginner-level Python (variables, functions, lists, using libraries) might be required to understand how the financial data is processed to output metrics.

- **What:** Attendees will be able to discover briefly about the XBRL language, hands-on techniques for getting data from SEC EDGAR's `companyfacts` API, combining data science and software engineering to validate data with Pydantic, extract key fundamental metrics from the API responses, calculate basic financial ratios, visualize financial trends, and learn the nuances of working with public financial data APIs, even internationally.

- **How:** This talk will be presented in a mixed-style of core financial concepts with live (fallback is prepared in case network errors) Python demonstrations in a Jupyter Notebook / Google Colaboratory. This talk will go through the entire process: selecting a company to visualize its financial health, techniques to ensure that the data is valid, and calculating financial metrics and ratios.

### Scope

- **I am NOT a financial advisor and this talk is for educational purposes only, I will NOT promote or recommend any specific assets, companies, products, and strategies, and this talk is NOT to be construed as any financial, investment, or trading advice**
- Advanced financial modeling, company valuations, and comprehensive ratio analysis are outside of the talk's scope
- This talk does not dive deep with parsing XBRL format
- This talk does not cover how to buy and/or sell securities
- All examples of this talk use historical data, past performance is not indicative of future performance

### Outline

Planned outline of the presentation:

- Introduction and Disclaimer (~3 minutes)
    - Quick self-introduction and an important disclaimer that I am not a financial advisor and this talk is not a financial advice
    - Why analyze company fundamentals with Python?
- The Data: SEC EDGAR, XBRL, and APIs (~4 minutes)
    - Overview of SEC, EDGAR system, and U.S. company filings (10-K)
    - Brief introduction to XBRL as the structured data standard
    - Focus on the `companyfacts` JSON API for XBRL-derived data
- Real-Life Scenario: Ensuring Data Quality with Pydantic (~3 minutes)
    - Why Pydantic and a quick overview of the Pydantic models for the API response
- Fetching and Validating Company Data (~3 minutes)
    - Use `requests` and `pydantic` to get and validate data for a sample U.S. company
    - Handle potential API or validation issues
- Finance Metrics Explanation & Extraction (~7 minutes)
    - Explanation of basic, core finance metrics: `Revenue`, `Net Income`, `Assets`, `Liabilities`, `Equity`
    - Extraction of the annual data, building the `pandas`'s `DataFrame` to showcase the data
    - Adapting to different XBRL tags (different derived JSON property) for the same financial concept, companies might not have the same schema
- Calculation of Finance Ratios (~3 minutes)
    - Explanation of finance ratios: `Net Profit Margin`, `Debt to Equity Ratio`
    - Calculation of the metrics
- Visualizing Trends (~2 minutes)
    - From the metrics and calculations, generating and showcasing plots with `matplotlib` / `seaborn`
- Internationalization and Data Nuances (~2 minutes)
    - How other countries (example: Japan has `EDINET`) has a different system, but with the same XBRL data structure, proving the skills and knowledge are transferrable
- Key Takeaways, Recap, Closing (~2 minutes)
    - Summary of the process, the tools, suggestions for future exploration
Notes:
I'm a first time PyCon HK speaker. Thank you for reading my proposal until the very end. I'm excited to contribute back to open source and to the community by sharing what I know about finance and/or software with Python in general!

Feel free to let me know if there's any feedback that I need to do!
What motivates you to submit this propos:
My finance journey started near the same time I discovered the world of computer programming. I started programming in the final year of junior high school, while my first investing journey was in the second year of senior high school. With my savings, I purchased my first stock, then watched it fall. That moment was shocking for me, and as a high-schooler who experienced a market downturn for the first time, it basically slashed my net worth and made me develop a slight fear of the finance world.

Years later, after entering the workforce and meeting many people, I realized that many people often find the finance world intimidating and they have the same fear as I had. It is often perceived as risky, confusing, full of "get rich quick" schemes and scams, inaccessible data, and a lot of difficult jargons. This "reputation" can make it feel intimidating and inaccessible, even though financial literacy is essential for everyone.

Understanding the fundamentals of public companies, how they operate and perform, how they report their performance is relevant in our data-driven world, whether for professional development or for personal interest. I realized that by leveraging Python as a bridge, it can transform the task of reading through official company's disclosures into an accessible, quantitative, and insightful process. In short, these are the goals of the session:

- Show how public companies report their financial state
- Show that anyone with basic Python skills can start to learn from this data that is taken from the official data source
- Show that while we focus on US data, the core Python and finance knowledge for data acquisition, validation, and analysis are valuable and transferable internationally
- Personally, I'd like to improve the general financial literacy about the finance world    

I want attendees to leave feeling more confident and equipped to use Python as a tool to better understand the financial information that "shapes" our world.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth:
From my talk, I'm going to emphasize the following points of why I think the topic is important for the Python community:

- Showcasing practical Python for one of the finance domain problems: being able to analyze and potentially automate company fundamental analysis with a public data and promoting data-driven approaches to understand companies
- Cross domain-knowledge sharing of software engineering and finance: being able to use Pydantic (a data validation library that is popular in the creation of web applications) to also be used to validate finance data
- Novelty: while the presentation is focused on getting the data from SEC API (for convenience), a brief introduction to XBRL (it is technically an XML-based language) will be conducted, so it is an additional knowledge for Python enthusiasts
What value will the audience gain?:
From my talk, I hope the audiences will go out of the room with these knowledge (among others):

- An understanding of how to access and validate US's public company financial data from the SEC EDGAR API
- Practical techniques to extract key fundamental metrics, and how to visualize the data in the form of charts
- The ability to calculate and interpret basic financial ratios
- An understanding of how global financial data is structured (different variations and different schemas), while specific APIs differ globally, the core skills are transferrable

Proposal title: IPList to BPFRule: A Python DDoS Mitigation Framework for Domain-Level Attacks via XDP_HOOK of bpfilter
Abstract: This paper presents a domain-specific DDoS mitigation approach combining DNS redirection, reverse proxy WAF, and kernel-level filtering with eBPF XDP via bpfilter. Instead of using BGP Flowspec, attacker IPs are identified at the origin, uploaded to a central IP list, and dynamically applied as XDP_HOOK rules using a Python-based service. This architecture enables efficient, low-resource blocking for phishing-injected gambling domains without requiring expensive infrastructure, making it ideal for organizations with limited network-layer control.
Description:
Introduction:
In recent years, Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks targeting previously compromised injected websites have become increasingly prevalent. This trend poses a significant threat to Indonesian web infrastructure, particularly domains under the .id top-level domain associated with governmental or institutional organizations. Unlike attacks that rely on specific Layer 7 pattern - such as SQL Injection or Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) - these DDoS attacks exploit volumetric or stateful protocol-layer weakness (e.g., OSI Layer 4 and Layer 7) without leaving standard application-layer signatures. Consequently, conventional Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) often fail to detect or mitigate the threat effectively, and attempting to do so can result in excessive resource consumption on the WAF itself. Mitigating such attacks typically requires volume-based or stateful traffic analysis tools capable of distinguishing between legitimate requests and malicious traffic patterns. While low-volume Layer 7 DDoS attacks may still be managed at the origin server level, doing so risks overwhelming the server’s firewall and web server stack - particularly when filtering rules impose high latency loading time then require the web server to have health checks that resulted in reload or restart. If the health check of the web server causes too many restarts it could have a bad effect on the site.
Another commonly used defense mechanism is BGP Flowspec, which enables volume-based traffic analysis and filtering at the network level [1]. While effective against high-bandwidth volumetric attacks, this method has limitations - it cannot mitigate stateful DDoS attacks that exploit the stateful connection layer 4 request. In such cases, traffic must be redirected to scrubbing center, where more sophisticated inspection and mitigation are performed. To execute filtering at these centers, one of the most advanced and increasingly adopted technologies is eBPF XDP (eXpress Data Path). XDP enables high-performance packet processing in the Linux kernel, allowing packets to be intercepted at the NIC driver level, thus avoiding unnecessary transitions to user space for blocking. This results in faster, more efficient mitigation [2].
XDP works by attaching hooks at low level in the network kernel stack, enabling the implementation of custom filtering logic using eBPF. However, most BGP Flowspec and XDP integrations are designed to protect specific IP addresses, not domain names. This approach is therefore unsuitable for organizations that do not own BGP Flowspec-enabled routers or need filtering on domain names. Furthermore, deploying this infrastructure solely to block domain-based attacks may lead to unnecessary overhead and resource use.
Instead of relying on BGP Flowspec in combination with XDP, this paper proposes an alternative approach that integrates domain name resolution via DNS, reverse proxy-based WAF, and XDP filtering using the bpfilter tool. By leveraging DNS resolution, domain-specific DDoS attacks can be mitigated without the need of BGP-based redirection. In this model, DNS is used to reroute targeted domain traffic to a reverse proxy server that is integrated with bpfilter XDP rules for rarely-stage packet filtering.
Furthermore, widely adopted reverse proxy WAF - such as Safeline or BunkerWeb - can be configured to route clean traffic to appropriate origin server after initial filtering. This layered approach not only enables domain-focused filtering at the kernel level, but also reduces the computational burden on the reverse proxy WAF by offloading early blocking to XDP. As a result, DDoS attacks against specific domains can be handled more efficiently with lower resource consumption, without requiring access to advanced routing infrastructure such as BGP Flowspec.  
Methodology:
To effectively mitigate DDoS attacks on specific domains, a volume-based traffic analysis system-similar in function to BGP Flowspec-is required. However, instead of implementing full-scale, low-level volume analysis mechanism, this solution adopts a simplified version that minimizes complexity and avoids kernel-level development.
Before detailing the meethod, the following are the key components that make up the solution:
- Volume-Based Analysis Tool at the origin server, which detects volumetric attacks and uploads attacker IPs to a centralized IP list (“Bucket IP List”).
- DNS A Record Redirection, pointing the targeted domain to a Reverse Proxy WAF (e.g. Safeline).
- iplist_to_bpfrule Linux Service, which executes a Python script to pull thousands of attacker IPs from the central Bucket IP List
- bpfilter XDP tool and service, responsible for enforcing the ruleset at the kernel level using XDP_HOOK
- safeline WAF as it's reverse proxy WAF
The Volume Based Analysis Tool runs on the origin server and monitors resource-intensive, volumetric HTTP behavior. In its original implementation, it blocked detected attacker IPs directly using the server’s firewall. However, as the volume of malicious IPs grew, this approach became problematic - it caused excessive rule loading and triggered frequent restarts due to health check failures.
To address this, this tool was redesigned to offload blocking to a reverse proxy layer. Once the attack threshold is surpassed, the origin no longer performs direct mitigation. Instead, it uploads the identified attacker IPs to cloud bucket (the “IP List”) and switches the targeted domain’s DNS A record to point to pre-configured Reverse Proxy WAF server.
The reverse proxy server (e.g., Safeline) forwards clean traffic to the origin server, while the initial filtering of malicious requests is handled at the kernel level using bpfilter XDP ruleset. In front of the reverse proxy, the bpfilter tool combined with iplist_to_bpfrule service dynamically injects XDP_HOOK rulesets based on attacker lists fetched from the bucket. This functionality is driven by iplist_to_bpfrule service, a Python-based daemon that periodically pulls new IPs and applies them to the ruleset using bpfilter.
This architecture allows for efficient L3/L4 blocking, reduces the resource burden on the WAF, and eliminates the need for high-cost BGP or scrubbing center infrastructure, making it suitable for smaller-scale or budget-conscious environments.

Proposal title: Leveraging BCC in Sandboxed MicroVMs for Malicious Package Analysis
Abstract: **eBPF** has gained widespread use in cloud-native environments for tracing, networking, and observability by allowing dynamic extension of Linux kernel functionality, eBPF poses potential security risks-particularly in shared environments such as containers. Containers share the host kernel, increasing the attack surface for kernel-level exploits. While VMs offer improved isolation, risk remain when orchestration is not under our control. This work explores using **microVMs**-specifically **Firecracker**-to securely run **python BCC-powered eBPF tools**. I demonstrate how to compile an **eBPF-capable kernel** for firecracker, configure Firecracker, and apply this setup for analyzing python malicious packages.
Description:
In recent years, **eBPF** has emerged as a powerful technology for dynamic kernel instrumentation in modern Linux environments. It enables developers to safely execute custom bytecode within the kernel, unlocking advanced capabilities for performance monitoring, security introspection, and tracing-all without modifying kernel source code or rebooting the system. In cloud-native ecosystems such as Kubernetes and containerized infrastructure, eBPF has seen widespread adoption for observability, network visibility, and threat detection.
However, the very strengths of eBPF-its deep kernel integration and privileged access-also critical security concerns. Deploying eBPF programs typically requires elevated privileges (e.g, root, CAP_BPF, CAP_PERFMON or CAP_NET_ADMIN [1]), introducing risk when running in shared or multi-tenant environments with shared kernel. Malicious actors could potentially abuse eBPF to gain insight into kernel internals or even exfiltrate sensitive data [2]. While containers offer isolation at the user space level, they share the same kernel, making them ill-suited for hosting untrusted eBPF programs for malicious package analysis due to heightened risk of kernel exploitation and container escape.
A more secure alternative lies in the use of virtual machines (VMs), which provide full kernel isolation. Yet, traditional VMs are often resource-intensive, slow to boot, and less control on the network side with low cost cloud providers. This is where **microVMs**, such as those powered by **Firecracker**, present a compelling solution: they combine the strong isolation properties of VMs with the lightweight and fast-boot characteristics of containers. MicroVMs run minimal kernels and images, making them ideal for sandboxing unsafe workloads such as malware package samples.
Despite their advantages, one significant limitation of  microVMs like Firecracker is that their default minimalist kernels lack eBPF compatibility due to missing kernel configurations and headers. Enabling dynamic tracing and observation within such environments requires deliberate customization.
In this work, I explore the integration of the **BCC (BPF Compiler Collection) Python-based library** within **Firecracker-powered microVM**. BCC simplifies the creation and deployment of eBPF programs via high-level abstractions and dynamic tracing scripts. I demonstrate how to compile a custom eBPF-enabled kernel, configure it for Firecracker, and run BCC scripts inside isolated microVMs to monitor and analyze potentially malicious activity.
This approach aims  to balance powerful observability with strong workload isolation, enabling scalable and secure dynamic analysis of untrusted or suspicious python package. Through this setup, I illustrate that BCC in a microVM-sandboxed environment offers a practical framework for malicious package behavior analysis, uniquely positioned at the intersection of performance, security, and flexibility. This kind of mechanism is good for security practicioners who cannot afford high cost sandboxing OS for analyzing malicious package and I would like to share my exploration with them as open source person.
References:
[1] L. Rize, Learning eBPF: Programming the Linux Kernel for Enhanced Observability, Networking, and Security. Sebastopol, CA, USA: O’Reilly Media, 2023. 
[2] Trend Micro, “How eBPF enabled Malware Works,” 2023. [Online]. Available: https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/id/security/news/threat-landscape/how-bpf-enabled-malware-works-bracing-for-emerging-threats. [Accessed: 01-Jun-2025]
What motivates you to submit this propos: I would likely to share my approach in doing Sandboxing Malicous Package Analysis with BCC and Firecracker with eBPF enabled kernel to open source security practicioners. I would love as a new open source person to contribute to open source security practicioners.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Understanding BCC and eBPF and how to securely analyze malicious package with BCC and eBPF enabled kernel inside Firecracker
What value will the audience gain?: Understanding a little bit of python, kernel space, and user space, and isolation mechanism like VMs or containers.

Proposal title: Mastering Observability: From Monitoring to Tracing with Prometheus, EFK, Jaeger & OpenTelemetry
Abstract: Unlock the power of modern observability tools to monitor, log, and trace your Kubernetes applications effectively! This hands-on workshop will guide you through the essential concepts and practical implementations of observability — from setting up Prometheus monitoring and custom metrics, to managing logs with the EFK stack, and enabling distributed tracing with Jaeger and OpenTelemetry. Whether you’re a developer, site reliability engineer, or DevOps enthusiast, this course will equip you with the skills to build robust, observable cloud-native systems.
Description:
What Will Be Covered
Episode 1: Introduction to Observability

Core concepts of Observability, Monitoring, Logging, and Tracing in modern software systems

Differences between Monitoring and Observability with Python applications in Kubernetes

Overview of popular Python-friendly tools for observability

Comparing monitoring approaches on Bare-Metal vs. Kubernetes environments running Python services

Episode 2: Prometheus - Setting Up Monitoring

Introduction to Prometheus architecture tailored for Python microservices

Setting up Prometheus in an EKS cluster for Python workloads

Installing kube-prometheus-stack with Helm and integrating it with Grafana for Python app metrics visualization

Writing and running basic PromQL queries on Python app metrics

Episode 3: Metrics and PromQL in Prometheus

Learning PromQL to query metrics generated by Python applications

Aggregating and analyzing Python application metrics using PromQL functions

Episode 4: Instrumentation and Custom Metrics

Instrumenting Python applications to expose custom metrics

Exploring Prometheus metric types: Counter, Gauge, Histogram, and Summary with Python examples

Writing custom metrics in Python using libraries like prometheus_client

Containerizing the instrumented Python app with Docker and deploying on Kubernetes

Setting up Alertmanager to create alerts based on Python app metrics

Episode 5: Logging with the EFK Stack

Understanding logging best practices for Python applications in distributed environments

Setting up the EFK stack (Elasticsearch, Fluentbit, Kibana) for centralized logging of Python apps on Kubernetes

Collecting and visualizing Python logs efficiently

Cleaning up resources post-workshop

Episode 6: Distributed Tracing with Jaeger

Introduction to distributed tracing concepts for Python microservices

Setting up Jaeger in Kubernetes using Helm for tracing Python service calls

Instrumenting Python services with OpenTelemetry SDK for tracing

Analyzing Python request flows and latencies in Jaeger UI

Environment cleanup after tracing setup

Episode 7: Unified Observability with OpenTelemetry

Deep dive into OpenTelemetry’s unified approach for metrics, logs, and traces in Python ecosystems

Comparing OpenTelemetry with traditional tools like Jaeger and Prometheus from a Python developer’s perspective

Multi-language support and integration options including Python SDKs

Step-by-step setup of OpenTelemetry in Kubernetes with Python app instrumentation
What motivates you to submit this propos: I submitted this proposal to bridge a knowledge gap that many Python developers face once their applications go into production—understanding what’s happening in live environments. Observability isn't just a backend concern anymore. With Python powering more microservices and APIs in cloud-native stacks, it’s crucial for Python developers to know how to monitor, log, and trace their applications. This workshop is designed to give them the real-world tools and hands-on experience they need to confidently manage their apps in Kubernetes.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: As Python applications increasingly power APIs, ML models, and microservices in production environments, observability becomes essential. Yet, many developers are unfamiliar with tools like Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, and Jaeger—or they struggle to apply them effectively to Python. This workshop is tailored to Python developers and shows them how to implement best practices for metrics, logging, and tracing within the Python ecosystem. It directly addresses a rising need in the community: how to ensure Python apps are visible, debuggable, and reliable in modern, distributed systems.
What value will the audience gain?:
Participants will leave with:

A strong foundation in observability concepts tailored for Python applications.

Hands-on skills using tools like Prometheus, Grafana, the EFK stack, Jaeger, and OpenTelemetry—all applied to Python workloads.

Practical experience instrumenting Python apps to expose and query custom metrics.

The ability to trace distributed calls in Python microservices and set up alerts based on real-time metrics.

A working, Kubernetes-based environment they can replicate for their own projects.

Most importantly, they’ll gain the confidence to take their Python services from “it runs on localhost” to “it runs in prod, and I know exactly how it’s performing.”

Proposal title: Building Org-Scale AI Agents
Abstract:
Most enterprises have data scattered across systems, security teams worried about AI access, and growing demands for smarter automation. Simple chatbots don't cut it anymore—organizations need agent systems that can handle complex workflows while meeting compliance requirements.
This session walks through a practical architecture using Python's FastAPI, Agentic Frameworks (Agno/LangGraph) handling the heavy lifting. 

We'll cover three agent patterns that work in production like hierarchical supervisors and swarm-style collaboration. The focus is on real implementation details—multi-tenancy through identity brokers, per-org vector stores, audit logging, and performance monitoring that actually helps. We'll end with a rollout plan that gets you from pilot to production.
Description: We’ll dig into the key decisions—from designing agents that talk to each other, to making sure they don’t break existing workflows. I’ll share patterns that worked well in production (like hierarchical supervisors and swarm-style collaboration), and cover real-world challenges. The focus is on what it really takes to move from demo to daily use—treating AI agents not just as clever tools, but as part of a maintainable, secure system.
Notes: This talk is mainly focussed on the best practices

- It also helps Python developers move from prototypes to real-world AI deployments.

Proposal title: From Commits to Community: Sustaining Open Source Through Collective Contribution
Abstract:
Open source is often celebrated for its code but the real magic lies in the people (that is community)  who build, support or contribute , and sustain it. While code contributions are essential, the long-term health of open source projects depends just as much on the collective effort of community builders, Programmers , documentation writers, designers, testers, event organizers, and advocates.

In this talk, I will explore what it really means to sustain open source beyond commits. Drawing from my experiences in community organizing and open source involvement, I will share insights on the unseen but vital roles that help projects thrive, how to create space for diverse contributions, and how we can foster inclusive, resilient communities around our projects and in open source.

Whether you are a maintainer, contributor, or someone curious about getting involved in open source, this talk will encourage you to rethink what “contribution” means and hopefully inspire you to support any open source in a new and meaningful ways.
Description:
Open source sustainability is  purely in terms of code: bug fixes, new features, and pull requests. But successful projects thrive because of the broader community that forms around them. This session will highlight the many ways individuals can contribute beyond code, and how these efforts build resilient, welcoming, and enduring projects.

We will discuss:

The  forms of contribution: documentation, translations, design, support, outreach, and more
Strategies for building and nurturing inclusive communities.

Real-world examples of projects that have flourished through diverse contributions.

Practical steps for maintainers to recognize and encourage all types of contributors

How to avoid burnout and foster a sense of shared ownership.

Attendees will leave with a deeper understanding of what it takes to sustain open source, actionable ideas for contributing in new ways, and inspiration to help their communities grow stronger together.

Target Audience:
 Open source maintainers, contributors (new and experienced), community managers, and anyone interested in the long-term success of collaborative software projects.

Takeaways:
Broaden your perspective on what it means to contribute.

Learn concrete strategies for community building.

Discover how to make your project more welcoming and sustainable for everyone.

Proposal title: AI for DevSecOps: Real-Time Threat Detection with Python
Abstract: In modern systems, logs and alerts move too fast for humans alone. This talk explores how Python and AI can work together to detect real-time security threats. We’ll walk through building lightweight anomaly detection pipelines using logs, metrics, and events—powered by Python libraries like scikit-learn, pandas, and OpenAI. From detecting credential stuffing to spotting CI pipeline tampering, you’ll see how smart automation can help DevSecOps teams find the signal in the noise—before it’s too late.
What motivates you to submit this propos: After dealing with multiple incidents where threats went unnoticed due to alert fatigue or noise, I began experimenting with ML in Python to help us catch early indicators of compromise. I want to share these techniques with others who face similar overload in security observability.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: As the threat landscape grows, security must become proactive. Python’s accessibility and rich ecosystem make it the perfect bridge between security operations and machine learning. This topic empowers Python developers to build smarter, faster, and more secure systems.
What value will the audience gain?: They’ll learn how to apply ML techniques to real security logs and alerts using Python. The session includes working examples, libraries, and architectural guidance that can help any team level up their threat detection capabilities—without buying expensive proprietary platforms.

Proposal title: Schrödinger’s Python Service, Is It Alive or Dead? Nobody Knows Until You Look.
Abstract:
Is your Python service truly alive, or has it silently died while everyone assumes it's fine?

This talk explores how the lack of observability in Python-based services creates a state akin to Schrödinger's cat — the service appears both alive and dead until someone opens the box. We'll discuss why observability is essential, and more importantly, why it's often neglected in real-world development and operations.

We'll take a practical look at implementing observability using **Logfire**, including examples of logging, tracing, and visualizing events. You'll also learn how to integrate with the **OpenAI API**, how to set up alerts that actually matter, and how to track key database metrics.

Whether you're a developer or an SRE, this session will provide you with concrete tools and strategies to bring your service out of the quantum box and into the realm of observable, reliable reality.
Description:
Observability is not a luxury — it's a necessity for running any production service. Yet many Python projects skip it due to time, complexity, or simple unfamiliarity.

In this talk, we’ll examine:
- Why observability matters for Python services
- Common reasons teams avoid or delay observability implementation
- Real-world usage of **Logfire** for capturing logs and metrics
- Integrating with external APIs like **OpenAI** for observability across boundaries
- Setting up meaningful **alerts**
- Monitoring **database metrics** in context

This session is designed to be practical, with concrete examples and code you can apply right away. You'll leave with the confidence and tools to make your Python service observable — and truly alive.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: observability

Proposal title: A Multi-Modal Approach to Item Moderation in Mercari
Abstract: This talk will present ItemModNet, an in-house multi-modal AI model for effective item moderation at Mercari - a Japanese online marketplace recently launched in Hong Kong. Developed primarily with ML frameworks in Python, ItemModNet combines text, image, price, and other structural data to predict fraudulent or policy-violating listings. Unlike generalized large-scale AI models such as the LLMs, ItemModNet is finely tuned to Mercari's unique and complex guidelines, surpassing traditional moderation methods in both precision and recall. By integrating domain-specific expertise with AI techniques, ItemModNet demonstrates the enduring value of specialized, smaller-scale models in effectively addressing nuanced, guideline-driven tasks.
Description:
Item moderation is essential for maintaining trust and safety on Mercari, as our marketplace handles millions of diverse listings daily. The major challenge is that moderation requires identifying fraudulent and non-compliant items while minimizing user friction. Over the years, Mercari has adopted various automated systems to aid this process, but the expansion and complexity of our marketplace demand continuous advancements to stay ahead of the ever changing situation.

To address the evolving challenge, we have developed ItemModNet, a multi-modal AI model optimized specifically for Mercari’s unique requirements. ItemModNet integrates diverse data modalities—such as item images, text (e.g., names and descriptions), and structured metadata (e.g., price, categories, and item conditions)—to create a comprehensive understanding of each listing. By integrating insights from these diverse modalities, ItemModNet also performs better than general-purpose large AI models like LLMs, which often struggle with the specificity required for domain-specific, guideline-driven moderation tasks.

As a smaller-scale, specialized model, ItemModNet is designed to meet the unique demands of Mercari’s item moderation policies. Built using common machine learning frameworks and trained on a proprietary dataset, the model reduces manual workload for operators as well as improving detection efficiency. While it is not an "industry-leading" solution, ItemModNet exemplifies the enduring value of smaller, customized AI systems in addressing intricate challenges that generalized models overlook. 

This initiative further demonstrates Mercari's commitment to advancing marketplace integrity through AI-driven innovation. By continually refining tools like ItemModNet, we aim to build a safer and more reliable experience for all our users.
What motivates you to submit this propos: To share how AI can help to enhance the trust and safety in the marketplace.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is the current go-to programming language for AI development. We would like to share to the community the capability of the models that we can build using Python AI frameworks.
What value will the audience gain?: Use cases of domain specific smaller models.

Proposal title: Unlocking the Power of Vibe Coding with MCP Servers: A Hands-On Guide
Abstract:
What if you could take your AI from just chatting and writing to actually doing stuff? Like, real-world tasks. Well, buckle up because the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is here to turn your language models into action heroes!
Imagine this: You’ve got an AI, but it’s not just answering your questions. It’s querying databases, fetching real-time data (like live Airbnb listings!), saving files, and even running custom tasks—all thanks to MCP.
This workshop will teach one how to enhance development workflow by integrating Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers with external data sources. Attendees will learn to automate tasks, store context in vector databases, and fetch meaningful context from external services like Google Drive and Airbnb to boost their development productivity. We'll provide a hands-on experience with MCP servers and show how they enable seamless interactions between AI models and external systems, making workflows faster and more efficient.
Description:
In this hands-on workshop, we’ll go beyond theory and build a real AI agent setup using MCP – Model Context Protocol – to create an extensible, plug-and-play ecosystem between LLMs and APIs.
We’ll start with the basics: setting up Claude Desktop or Cursor IDE, wiring up an MCP server (Qdrant) to persist generated code, and then extending the system with a second tool (e.g., Airbnb search or Google Maps). Along the way, we'll cover:
* How MCP clients and servers interact
* STDIO and Server-Sent Events transport layers
* Writing and running multi-server configs in JSON
* Saving & retrieving LLM responses via Qdrant vector DB (RAG)
* Building custom tools to expose your own APIs to the LLM
This is "vibe coding" in action – collaborative, contextual, intelligent development where your model remembers, learns, and integrates seamlessly.
Workshop Agenda:
1. Introduction to MCP Servers (15 minutes)
* Overview of MCP: What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)? Why is it important for modern development workflows?
* Key Components of MCP:
* Client, Server, Transport Layer, and Protocol.
* How these components work together for enhanced model context and interaction.
* Real-world Use Cases: Discuss how MCP can help in common scenarios like task automation, integrating databases, and fetching external data.
2. Setting Up and Configuring MCP Servers (25 minutes)
* Demo of MCP Server Setup:
* Walk through how to set up an MCP server with an example like Qdrant (a vector database).
* Hands-on Activity: Attendees will follow along to configure their own MCP server using a JSON configuration file.
* Integrating External Services: How to connect MCP with Google Drive, Dropbox, or other cloud-based services to fetch/store data.
* Structuring JSON Files: Best practices for writing a well-organized MCP configuration that supports multiple servers.
3. Building a Real-World Use Case: Automating Tasks with MCP (30 minutes)
* Example Use Case: Build an agent using MCP to automate tasks and store/retrieve data using a vector database like Qdrant.
* Hands-on Activity:
* Attendees will use MCP to integrate services like Airbnb and Qdrant, automating repetitive tasks and generating context-aware responses.
* Example tasks: Automating fetching and storing data related to vacation rentals and previous code templates.
* Vibe Coding in Action: How MCP servers can enhance Vibe coding by enabling seamless task execution and context retrieval for future coding sessions.
4. Best Practices for Optimizing MCP Workflow (20 minutes)
* Optimizing Transport Layers: Discuss tips on enhancing the speed and reliability of communication between servers and clients.
* Troubleshooting Common Issues: How to handle errors, debug MCP server setups, and optimize your workflow.
* Structure and Efficiency: How to organize your JSON files and handle multiple servers in a single file for better scalability.
5. Q&A and Open Discussion (20 minutes)
* Open the floor for attendees to ask questions, provide feedback, and share experiences.

By the end of this workshop, participants will:
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of MCP and how it works.
2. Gain hands-on experience with setting up and configuring MCP servers.
3. Learn how to integrate vector databases and external APIs into their workflow using MCP.
4. Automate tasks and retrieve meaningful context for more efficient coding using MCP.
5. Implement best practices for managing and optimizing MCP workflows.
* A fully working MCP setup with Qdrant + Claude
* A personalized AI coding assistant that remembers your code patterns
* Enough knowledge to build and expose your own APIs via MCP
What motivates you to submit this propos: This proposal was driven by a simple idea: LLMs are powerful, but they’re even more powerful when they can interact with APIs, remember context, and automate real tasks. I’ve personally seen how integrating tools like Qdrant and Google Maps via MCP can transform a language model from a reactive assistant into an active coding partner. The motivation here is to demystify the process of building intelligent, extensible AI systems and show people that this isn’t just the domain of big tech — anyone can do it with the right tools and knowledge.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Many Python developers already work with LLMs, but few are fully tapping into agent-based architectures that persist context, integrate with databases, or use dynamic APIs. This workshop equips Python developers to build modular, action-oriented AI systems — a massive leap from stateless prompt-response models. By learning how to wire up agents with MCP, the Python community can build tools that truly augment development workflows, automation tasks, and more.
What value will the audience gain?:
Attendees will leave with:

A fully functional MCP setup, connected to Claude or Cursor, and wired to tools like Qdrant and Airbnb.

Hands-on experience building and configuring agents using real JSON config files and transport protocols (STDIO, SSE).

The knowledge to expose their own APIs to LLMs and persist/retrieve data through vector stores.

An understanding of RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) in action, customized for their dev needs.

A real glimpse into the future of “vibe coding” — where the model collaborates with you, remembers your code, and adapts over time.

This isn’t just theory — by the end of the session, every participant will have a working, extensible AI dev assistant running on their machine.

Proposal title: MCP for dummies: Feed more context to LLM
Abstract:
Providing the right context to large language models is challenging. Every integration—whether accessing local files, connecting to Google Calendar, or querying internal databases—requires custom work. Each tool connection becomes a separate, manual effort. This is where MCP comes in. Model Context Protocol (MCP), in simple terms, is a universal adapter for AI models that need external context. It standardizes how context is passed to models, making it easier to build and manage these connections.

In this workshop session, we will not only focus on how to get started with MCP, but I will also outline how to build MCP Agents using your own MCP Server tools and the MCP Client UI with Streamlit. At the end of my talk, we will also discuss the security issues associated with MCP and how one can mitigate those.
Description:
Outline of my talk- breakdown of the 90 minutes:

- Issues with Large language models and discuss the pain points for the need of MCP (3 min)

Proposal title: Structural Pattern Matching with Python
Abstract: Python 3.10 introduced structural pattern matching, a powerful and elegant feature that dramatically improves code readability and reduces boilerplate when dealing with complex data structures. This talk will dive into the syntax and capabilities of match statements, demonstrating how they offer a more expressive and maintainable alternative to lengthy if-elif-else chains and nested conditional logic. Attendees will learn how to effectively leverage pattern matching for tasks like data validation, command parsing, and state management, ultimately writing cleaner and more Pythonic code.
Description: Unleash the power of Python with structural pattern matching. Learn how to streamline complex logic, improve code readability, and handle diverse data structures efficiently. Discover the practical applications and best practices of this exciting new feature.

Proposal title: MCP vs APIs: Standardizing AI Agent Integrations
Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are revolutionizing AI, but to be truly useful, they must interact seamlessly with external data sources, services, and tools. Traditionally, this was done via APIs, but now a new open standard—the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—is changing the game. MCP standardizes how AI applications provide context and invoke tools, enabling more dynamic, interoperable AI agents.

In this talk, we’ll explore what MCP is, how it compares to traditional APIs, and why it’s poised to become the USB-C port of AI application integration. Attendees will learn the architecture of MCP, including its client-server model, primitives like tools and resources, and its unique runtime discovery feature. We’ll also demystify API basics and contrast the general-purpose nature of APIs with the AI-focused design of MCP.

You’ll walk away understanding how MCP enhances AI agent capabilities by enabling standardized, discoverable, and extensible integrations—while often leveraging existing APIs under the hood. This session is perfect for Python developers, AI practitioners, and anyone interested in the future of AI tooling and interoperability.
Description:
What Will You Learn?

The architecture and design principles behind the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

How MCP standardizes interaction patterns between AI agents and external services

The three core MCP primitives: tools, resources, and prompt templates

Key differences and similarities between MCP and traditional RESTful APIs

How MCP enables dynamic capability discovery at runtime

Real-world examples of MCP servers wrapping existing APIs (GitHub, Google Maps, Spotify, etc.)

Why MCP is a game-changer for building scalable, maintainable AI assistants
Notes:
Who Should Attend?

Python developers building AI applications and assistants

AI engineers and researchers interested in AI integration patterns

Developers curious about emerging open standards in AI tooling

Anyone wanting to understand how to architect LLM-powered services that interact with real-world data and tools

Technical Requirements:

Familiarity with Python and REST APIs helpful but not required

Interest in AI, large language models, or software integration

No prior knowledge of MCP required — all concepts will be explained from the ground up
What motivates you to submit this propos: I’m motivated by the desire to introduce the Python community to a groundbreaking open standard — the Model Context Protocol (MCP) — that is reshaping how AI agents, especially those powered by large language models, integrate with external data and services. While APIs have long been the go-to method, MCP addresses critical gaps by offering a standardized, discoverable, and AI-centric way to connect tools and context dynamically. Sharing this knowledge empowers developers and AI practitioners to build more scalable, flexible, and maintainable AI systems aligned with the future of AI tooling.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python developers are at the forefront of AI and machine learning innovation, often building complex applications that require seamless integration with external services and data sources. Understanding MCP equips Python developers with a powerful new protocol that complements and enhances traditional APIs, specifically tailored for AI agents. MCP simplifies integration through standardized primitives and runtime discovery, reducing the need for custom adapters and accelerating development. This knowledge will help Python developers create more robust AI-powered applications and stay ahead in a rapidly evolving ecosystem.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will gain a solid understanding of the Model Context Protocol’s architecture, core primitives, and its dynamic discovery capabilities — all essential for designing AI agents that interact efficiently with real-world data and tools. They will learn how MCP differs from and builds upon traditional API paradigms, how to leverage MCP servers (many of which wrap existing APIs), and practical insights into using MCP today with popular services. Ultimately, the audience will leave equipped to implement scalable, interoperable AI integrations and contribute to the future of AI tooling innovation.

Proposal title: Security in the Age of LLMs: Small act >> Big leaps
Abstract:
In a world captivated by breakthrough models and sweeping AI promises, it's easy to overlook the quieter, daily choices that shape our collective future. Security in the age of Large Language Models (LLMs) isn’t just about firewalls or compliance checklists; it’s about the small, intentional acts embedded into our workflows, documentation, and community norms.

As a maintainer of [DataJourney](https://github.com/DataJourneyHQ/DataJourney), I’ve learned that when working at the intersection of open source and AI, security is not a solo pursuit; it’s a shared habit. 

In this talk, I’ll share stories, patterns, and practical steps that reflect how we can embed security not through fear, but through responsibility, reproducibility, and thoughtful defaults. We'll explore how open ecosystems can cultivate trust with small, consistent contributions from everyone involved.
What motivates you to submit this propos: My day-to-day revolves around building, securing, and repeating it all over again. I am ready to share a few nuggets to make the journey for others simpler.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: We are in the era of LLM, safe to say security is language agnostic and needs urgent attention
What value will the audience gain?: Real examples, practical guidance

Proposal title: High Dimensions, Low Hassle: Solving the Curse with Python
Abstract: High-dimensional datasets are common in modern data science workflows but they come at a cost. From bloated training times to overfitting and inscrutable patterns, the “curse of dimensionality” can quietly sabotage even the most promising machine learning projects. In this session, we'll demystify what this curse really is, why it matters, and how you can break free from it using Python. Through visual examples and practical code, we’ll explore dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and autoencoders. You'll see how these methods simplify data while preserving structure, improve model performance, and reveal hidden insights that are otherwise lost in the noise. Whether you're a beginner aiming to better understand high-dimensional data, or an experienced practitioner looking to optimize and interpret complex datasets, this talk will give you practical tools to make your models faster, cleaner, and smarter.
Description:
High-dimensional data is increasingly common in modern data science, but it often introduces more complexity than value. With too many features, models become slower to train, more prone to overfitting, and harder to interpret. In this talk, we’ll explore practical strategies to manage and simplify high-dimensional datasets, tackling what’s known as the “curse of dimensionality.” We'll begin by unpacking this curse explaining why high-dimensional spaces can lead to sparse data, distorted distance measures, and misleading patterns that reduce the effectiveness of machine learning models. This foundational understanding will set the stage for discussing how to address these challenges through dimensionality reduction.

We’ll dive into some of the most widely used dimensionality reduction techniques in Python, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), and neural network–based autoencoders. Each method will be introduced with its strengths, limitations, and ideal use cases. Through clear, concise code examples using libraries like scikit-learn, umap-learn, and keras, you’ll see how these techniques reduce data complexity while preserving the underlying structure.

A key focus will be on how dimensionality reduction improves model efficiency reducing training time, simplifying hyperparameter tuning, and enhancing generalization by removing noise and redundancy. We'll also look at how it can aid data exploration, with visual examples that show how reducing dimensions helps uncover hidden patterns and relationships that are hard to detect in raw feature spaces.

The session concludes with real-world applications, offering tips on how to incorporate dimensionality reduction into your own data pipelines. Whether you're just starting with machine learning or looking to refine existing workflows, this talk will provide actionable insights to help you better manage complex datasets and build more robust, interpretable models.

Proposal title: What does it take to create a language of your own in Python?
Abstract:
Ever wondered how to create your own domain-specific language tailored to your needs?

This session explores how to build a programming language that lets users write code using natural language. Designed to be fun, intuitive and easy to use, the language is crafted for young learners especially those for whom English is not a first language. Built with Python, the system parses and interprets natural language into executable code. I’ll share the design challenges, key insights and lessons learned from creating a language that’s user-centered.
Description:
This session is for anyone curious about building your own little domain-specific languages, exploring new ways to teach programming or just crafting code that speaks your own language, literally.

Inspired by my working with an organization that taught coding to children and talks at PyCon APAC, I asked: What if programming could be made more accessible with a language tailored to children? 

The talk will cover:

**Language Design**
- Making decisions around syntax depending on the purpose.

**Architecture Choices**
- Interpreter vs compiler: which architecture best fits for your need?
- Parsing libraries: tools available such as PLY, Lark.

**Technical Implementation**
- Building the lexer, parser, and interpreter and handling errors using Python.

**Demo**
- The language in action.

**Future Directions**
- Adding support for more languages, introducing to wider community.
Notes:
I've attended several PyCon events and after being inspired by many of the talks, I'm excited to submit my first PyCon talk proposal. If selected, I hope to inspire others and give back to the community that has given me so much.

I will require a visa to travel to Hong Kong in order to attend and present at the conference. Please let me know if you need any additional information or documentation to assist with the visa process.
What motivates you to submit this propos:
I used to work at an organization that taught programming to children with some basic understanding of English. However, I’ve often wondered about children from rural areas or those who struggle with English. How can we support them?
While there are ongoing efforts to make coding more accessible, I believe we can do more. I believe programming should be accessible to everyone, even for non-native English speakers. I want to share how we can bridge that gap using natural language and how someone can build a domain-specific language for their own purpose.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: By exploring how Python can be used to create domain-specific languages, we open the door to new ideas and customized tools for various use cases. Introducing the concept of natural language programming encourages others to build similar projects that can enhance their own learning and make programming more accessible in their community.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will learn key considerations for creating their own programming language, including useful tools for parsing and building interpreters, as well as potential challenges they may encounter along the way.

Proposal title: Circuit Tracing in Transformers: Peeking Inside the Black Box
Abstract:
I will explain what circuit tracing is in large language models like Gemma. It's a new way to understand how models answer questions by looking inside them and checking which neurons activate when. Anthropic open sourced a library called circuit-tracer and also the website Neuronpedia, which helps us find neurons linked to real-world concepts like "Texas" or "capital".

I'll show how this works with a live demo from their Jupyter notebook. We'll see what nodes and supernodes are, and how they connect to form reasoning paths in the model. This can help us debug, understand, and make models safer.

Proposal title: Building Bridges Across Asia: The Role of the Python Asia Organization (PAO)
Abstract: The Python Asia Organization (PAO) is a newly established non-profit organization dedicated to fostering collaboration and growth among Python communities across East and Southeast Asia. This session explores PAO’s mission, its early achievements, and its potential to shape the future of Python programming in the region.
Description:
The Python Asia Organization (PAO) was founded to support and empower Python communities across East and Southeast Asia. PAO’s mission is to cultivate leadership, foster collaboration, and promote inclusive, sustainable growth for Python programming in the region. By connecting local organizers and providing shared resources, PAO aims to build a stronger and more united Python ecosystem.

This session will cover:

* PAO’s Mission: The vision of fostering collaboration, leadership, and sustainability among diverse Python communities.
* Early Achievements: Key milestones during its establishment, including global and regional initiatives.
* Future Goals: Plans for leadership development, resource-sharing platforms, and support for flagship events like PyCon APAC.
* Challenges and Opportunities: Current hurdles such as funding, organizational scaling, and fostering cross-border connections.

The session will conclude with a 10-minute discussion, inviting participants to contribute ideas, propose solutions, and explore opportunities to strengthen Python communities through PAO.

This talk will be delivered in English.
What motivates you to submit this propos: We are motivated by the belief that stronger connections among Python communities in Asia can unlock immense potential for learning, collaboration, and innovation. As a newly formed organization, the Python Asia Organization (PAO) aims to address the fragmentation across regional communities and provide a platform where ideas, resources, and leadership can be shared. This proposal is an opportunity to introduce our vision to a broader audience, learn from others, and invite participation from those who care about building inclusive, sustainable Python ecosystems.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python thrives because of its vibrant global community—but regions like East and Southeast Asia have diverse, active groups that often remain disconnected from each other. Highlighting efforts to unify and uplift these communities not only strengthens the regional network but contributes to the overall resilience and diversity of the global Python ecosystem. This topic promotes collaboration, mutual support, and the development of new leaders—all essential for the long-term growth of the community.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will gain practical insights into the formation and goals of a cross-border nonprofit, understand the benefits and challenges of regional collaboration, and discover ways to apply similar practices in their own communities. They will also learn how to contribute to or leverage PAO’s initiatives—such as leadership training, shared resources, and event support—and leave with concrete ideas for fostering more sustainable, inclusive community growth in their own local or regional contexts.

Proposal title: Demystify vLLM: introducing the de-facto LLM inference engine for private AI
Abstract:
With the rise of public cloud services, most people began using LLMs online. However, in August 2025, hundreds of thousands of chat were leaked and surfaced on Google, raising serious concerns about whether it’s still safe to share confidential information with online LLMs. As a result, growing numbers of users are looking to deploy their own models—either in home labs or enterprise environments—to maintain full control.

Ollama has been the most popular self-hosted LLM solution, but it isn’t designed for large-scale deployments. In contrast, vLLM has recently emerged as a de facto standard for high-performance LLM inference serving.

In this talk, we’ll compare vLLM and Ollama and highlight the advantages of vLLM. We’ll also explore the technical inference optimization techniques behind vLLM that reduce GPU compute and memory usage. Finally, we’ll demonstrate how to use and configure vLLM within a Python script.
What motivates you to submit this propos: More and more people are interested to host their own LLM, but yet don't know the technical details behind LLM serving engine.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: vLLM is a very popular open source project in LLM serving and it is based on python. The python community should know about this project.
What value will the audience gain?: Audience will learn the technical concepts behind the optimizations used in vLLM, and learn how to scale LLM deployment beyond Ollama.

Proposal title: From Chaos to Harmony: A GenAI Solution to Music Library Clutter
Abstract: Ever opened your music folder only to be greeted by a chaotic mix of album and track names that trigger your inner OCD? This talk explores the journey from manual cleanup to building a Python tool that brings order to musical chaos. By harnessing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Large Language Models (LLMs), and natural language processing (NLP), the project intelligently standardizes music libraries across diverse naming conventions and languages. The presentation focuses on the creative process, core AI concepts, and key lessons learned, tracing the path from tedious folder cleaning to an automated, AI-powered solution.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I was invited by a colleague and thought it would be a fun opportunity to share a personal project that combines my interests in music, automation, and generative AI. The process of turning a tedious manual task into something creative and useful with Python was rewarding, and I hope others will find it inspiring as well.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: This topic showcases how Python can be used alongside modern AI concepts like RAG and LLMs to solve everyday problems in creative ways. It highlights the practical application of AI and NLP in personal projects, encouraging the community to experiment and innovate beyond traditional use cases.
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will learn how to approach real-life problems with generative AI and Python, gain insights into integrating RAG and LLMs for automation, and be inspired to tackle their own “pet peeve” projects. They’ll also see how even simple ideas can evolve into engaging, impactful solutions.

Proposal title: Make use of Tox in your CI workflow
Abstract:
Are you tired of your code working in your environment, but failing when your teammate tries to run it? Are you tired of typing commands into your bash terminal again and again just to run your test cases? Are you tired of pushing your code to a shared repo, just to find out it failed the CI checks put in place by the repo's admin?

If you've ever encountered any of these situations, you may benefit from having tox in your CI workflow. With tox, you can set up virtual environments to automatically run your format checks and test cases - all in a single file. It's a simple and elegant solution that can save you and your team time and frustration.

Proposal title: What are AI pipeline frameworks good for?
Abstract: So, you want to build an AI-powered application in Python. In addition to the UI and database you would need in any application, you will of course need LLM deployments to call and prompts engineered to generate the desired output. Yet, with all of these elements in place, an AI application presents distinctive challenges for coordinating the interaction of LLMs and user data. A toy example that fills a few user-inputted variables into a prompt for use with a single LLM deployment endpoint requires only a few dozen lines of backend code. But what if you want to be able to swap between different models, deployments, or APIs? And how will you handle problems such as hitting quota limits or encountering irregularities in LLM output, or test how you process inputs and outputs? Or what if you want to build a more complex AI system that enriches the model's context (RAG) or can make its own calls to various tools in response to user requests (agents): which data sources and tools will you connect to, and how? Several Python packages -- including LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and PydanticAI -- claim to offer end-to-end frameworks for building application-ready AI pipelines and agents. Through a systematic comparison of their different features and structures, alongside the option of rolling a solution oneself, this talk will consider how using these frameworks might, or might not, make it easier to answer some of the challenging questions involved in building an AI application.
What motivates you to submit this propos: In my own experience writing the Python backend for an AI web application for past year and a half, I've had to tackle a series of problems that I think are general for this type of development. I've taken the road of iteratively building proprietary packages, rather than using one of the existing open source frameworks. I want to make this talk an opportunity to reflect on that choice by looking at what sorts of benefits existing packages offer.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python remains the go-to scripting language for AI engineering, and so I expect that a substantial number of members of the HK Python community who might attend PyCon are involved or interested in AI app development. They thus might have or will confront the challenges I'll cover and might use one of the frameworks I'll compare (or might consider writing one for themselves, as I did).
What value will the audience gain?: The audience will come away with an understanding of core problems and alternative solutions in building AI pipeline in Python. For those who have so far only built prototypes or learning projects, they'll be introduced to some of the considerations for building production-ready AI that they might not have been previous aware of. For those who are working on sophisticated AI apps, they'll gain some insight on the benefits they might gain from alternative frameworks.

Proposal title: Beyond Words: Exploring the Minds of Large Concept Models
Abstract:
In this talk, we’ll see how LCMs represent a major evolution from Large Language Models. While LLMs predict text by chaining together tokens, LCMs operate at a much deeper level—mapping and reasoning with abstract concepts like regret, curiosity, morality, and purpose. I’ll walk through how these models decompose high-level human ideas, show how tools like Meta’s Sonar test conceptual depth, and demonstrate how LCMs can summarize, generate, and even empathize.

The objective is to introduce, explain, and demonstrate how LCMs go beyond traditional language models by understanding and reasoning about human concepts—such as emotions, intentions, causality, and abstract ideas—paving the way for more intelligent, intuitive, and human-aligned AI systems.

Proposal title: Search matters: Engineering search systems that actually work
Abstract:
Large language models face fundamental limitations, including outdated training data, context window constraints, and a tendency to hallucinate. While vector similarity search is a popular solution through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), simple cosine similarity often fails to capture the nuanced relevance needed for high-quality LLM responses. 

This talk explores how search capabilities can enable your LLMs to provide accurate responses. We examine how sophisticated retrieval methods work through hybrid search combining dense and sparse retrieval, semantic reranking, and external memory using Qdrant Vector Database - Python client. We demonstrate how search becomes the critical bridge between knowledge and real-world information needs.
What motivates you to submit this propos: Last time at PyCon APAC 2024 in Indonesia, I delivered a talk on RAG. Many attendees started building RAG pipelines with LLMs afterward. However, it's important to understand that search is more than just RAG—it can be applied in various ways. This motivated me to propose a follow-up session on understanding why search matters in grounding LLM responses.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: I picked this topic because everyone's obsessing over embeddings and RAG while completely ignoring whether their search helps users. After building search systems that real people use, I've seen too many teams nail the technical implementation but fail at the basics, like understanding what users actually want. This talk covers the full journey from messy user queries to satisfied users, not just the vector similarity part everyone else is talking about.
What value will the audience gain?:
- When to use search for LLMs. 
- Re-ranking techniques for Search
- Personalized vs Recommendation-based Search

Proposal title: Splink for Enterprise-Grade Probabilistic Record Linkage
Abstract: Entity resolution is the hidden keystone of every modern data platform: marketing integration, fraud detection, and golden-record MDM all depend on knowing when two rows actually describe the same real-world person or entity. Traditional rule-based or fuzzy-string methods crumble once data volumes and DQ issues grow. Splink is an open-source Python library that brings the statistically principled Fellegi-Sunter model to the PyData stack, allowing tens-of-millions of records to be linked in minutes. This talk will go over how Splink implements blocking, comparison levels, EM training, and clustering.
Description:
Problem framing – real examples where duplicate customers break dashboards and compliance; when exact joins fails in real-world use cases.

Fellegi-Sunter – m/u probabilities, λ prior, match-weight formula, and the role of expectation-maximisation.

Splink deep dive – blocking rules, comparison levels, EM training, inference, and clustering

Live demo – link 50k synthetic retail-bank accounts in a single-node Spark session, then aggregate total-relationship-balance to show business impact
Notes: I have delivered this material at DurianPy (PH); the demo runs in less than a minute s on a laptop with Spark 3 + Splink. I can share the slides and other materials to the attendee after the talk.
What motivates you to submit this propos: I've seen firsthand how challenging entity resolution can be in production systems, and how Splink makes this more approachable for data engineers and analysts. I want to share what I’ve learned and help others avoid the common pitfalls when tackling record linkage problems.
Why is this topic important for the Pyth: Python is widely used for data processing, but scalable entity resolution often gets overlooked in typical toolkits. Splink bridges this gap with a performant, open-source solution grounded in solid statistical theory.
What value will the audience gain?: Attendees will walk away with a practical understanding of probabilistic record linkage, the principles behind Splink, and how to integrate it into their own workflows.

Proposal title: 從script到應用：用 Python 建立一個自動化 AI 程式設計 Workflow bot
Abstract:
AI 編程助手功能強大，但係不斷重複嘅copy and paste同管理對話卻嚴重消耗住我哋嘅生產力如果可以用一個智能嘅 Python 機器人嚟自動化整個工作流呢？

喺今次演講中，我會展示一個真實嘅項目：一個由零開始構建嘅 GUI 自動化工具，用於同 Cursor 、 Trae 、 Windsurf 等多個 AI 助手進行互動。我哋會由一個簡單嘅腳本開始，一步步將佢演進為一個健壯、可分發嘅桌面應用。
